utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today's Monday, the 5th of May, 2008. We are resuming the proceedings in this case. I'd like to greet the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, as well as the accused, and I see that all the accused are with us today. Before I give the floor to one of the parties if they wish to raise an administrative matter, I would like to say the following: This week we'll have first of all an opening statement today, and for the other three days this week we'll have a witness, a witness called by Mr. Prlic's Defence, and the Prlic Defence told us that they needed five hours to examine the witness in chief. If two and a half hours are allocated for the cross-examination of the other Defence counsel, that would give a total of seven and a half hours for the Defence to start with, plus five hours for the cross-examination by the Prosecution, and in total that's 12 and a half hours without taking into account Judges' questions or procedural matters. This week we'll finish on Thursday at 6.30, and therefore it is very likely that the witness will have to come back on Tuesday, the 13th of May, because the 12th of May is a Bank Holiday, unless, of course, the Prlic Defence uses less than five hours. Of course, Mr. Karnavas is the only one who can tell us anything about this matter. Are you still requesting or planning to examine this witness for five hours, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the court. As of this moment, the answer to that question is yes. However, and it is a big however, we are in the process of streamlining our questioning and reducing the number of documents that we wanted to introduce in order to achieve our objective within this week and not having to bring the witness over for some other -- for some other day. So we will do everything we possibly can. We also might be able to speak with some of our colleagues. We understand some of them may not have any questioning, in which case I think that we might be able to accommodate everyone in this courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Do the representatives of the Prosecution have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. No, we have nothing at this time. We'd just rather get started. There may be some matters tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, let me turn to you. If I understand correctly, your client is going to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. In keeping with the Trial Chamber's ruling with respect to the hours, we do understand the logistics that -- and the problems that the Court has. However, we also had to make some adjustments of our own, and having consulted extensively, we have decided that Mr. Prlic would provide a statement in lieu of taking the stand and testifying, and that would save approximately one month of time. But be that as it may, he is prepared. We believe the statement can be delivered today in its entirety if we commence as quickly as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Mr. Karnavas, I have a question in this respect with some surprise. I find here enormous volumes of documents. Now -- and they -- on the head of it, it says statement of Jadranko Prlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Now, I wonder procedurally how this comes in because you're quite aware of the fact that this declaration of Mr. Prlic will not be evidence in any way, and he cannot be cross-examined, of course, and is it your idea to introduce documents on which the person who introduces them cannot be cross-examined? I would like you to clarify your view on the procedural situation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. If you -- very well. The statement is presented in a fashion in which he makes references to documents. Some are in evidence already, so that should answer your question. If it is in evidence, it is evidence. The documents, that is. Others may be coming into evidence through other witnesses. I don't share your opinion that even an unsworn statement is not evidence. It has less weight, but you may decide, and maybe that is your position, and we'll do the research, and now that we know that your position is that it is not evidence, we'll see what -- what the jurisprudence says exactly on that point. It's my opinion it may have less weight. But of course we have been put in a position where we can't have our cake and eat it too. We can't put on our full defence and meet the demands, the hourly demands, that have been put upon us. Regrettably that was a decision that was made by this Trial Chamber because, I suspect, the completion strategy and the Security Council's need to close this place down as quickly as possible. So we're trying to accommodate. But that's how these documents are being used, as references to the -- to his particular statement. I fully recognise that through his statement, through his statement, and this is perhaps more to the -- to answer your question, through his statement documents cannot come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That was the clarification I was seeking there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And I agree that the question of evidence is open. It's the mercy of the Chamber, I was tempted to say, but it's certainly a matter of mercy but of appreciation, dutiful appreciation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. And I do appreciate your concern. Thank you very much, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. In order for those who follow our proceedings to understand what's going on, I'm going to read paragraph (B) of Rule 84 bis of the Rules that states that: "The Trial Chamber shall decide on the probative value of the statement, if any." Mr. Prlic, you have the floor. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. [Interpretation] Bearing in mind your decision on how much time the Defence is allowed to present our case, I have decided to offer this brief presentation. For the most part, I was about to address all the same issues during my own testimony. Bearing in mind the fact that I am taking the floor at the outset of the Defence case, I will be announcing some of our theories which we will be elaborating on over the next weeks through our evidence. In order to save time, I will try to avoid repeating what is already in the interview that I gave that the Chamber has already admitted apart from maybe some sections that require further elucidations. What I'm trying to say at the outset is this: There was no joint criminal enterprise such as alleged by the OTP. The intention that guided me in my work was pure as driven snow. I contributed to our Defence, to organising civilian life, and to building up Bosnia and Herzegovina or a possible Bosnia and Herzegovina. I never, in any way, committed any crimes, nor did I encourage the commission of any crimes, nor am I aware of the fact that any of the members of the provisional bodies of our executive at the time were involved in anything like this. Quite the contrary, in fact. We did everything to alleviate the consequences of war and destruction, and we took all the steps required to see the perpetrators of those crimes punished. As I said during my initial appearance four years ago, I'm not guilty under any of the counts of the indictment. I sympathise with all the victims of this war. I myself, after all, are in a way one of its victims. As I said before, my defence, too, represents the victims. My defence, too, wants to see those responsible punished. In my presentation, I will take a chronological approach combining such information as I had at the time certain things were happening. I will also use additional information gleaned for the most part from the OTP's evidence or from the evidence that will likely be used by one of the other Defence teams. This is something that I learned at a later stage. This will give us a rounded-out picture of what happened. When I spoke to the OTP, objectively speaking, I was in no position to understand the overall picture such as I do now. I will tell you about Bosnia and Herzegovina such is as it was within the Yugoslav Federation. I will tell you about the multi-party elections. I will tell you about the national issue arising at the time as a fundamental issue. I will tell you about the winds of war in Slovenia and Croatia. I will tell you about the chaos that prevailed in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I will tell you about the dilemma based at the time stay in Yugoslavia or go our own way. I will tell you about the then-existing administrative system. I will tell you about the formation of the Croatian communities and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the setting up of the HVO army and the provisional executive organ of the HZ HB, the reasons for the setting up of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the clash with the BH army in some of the free territory. I will also tell you about war crimes. I will tell you about my role prior to enduring the actual conflict. I will also try to provide further elucidations in relation to my interview with the OTP that -- there are things that I didn't have a chance to say in relation to a total of 24 different subjects that the OTP had served on me two months before the interview. Finally, I will address my alleged role in the joint criminal enterprise. I will be using the indictment itself to deal with this subject. Your Honours, you are familiar with my personal details, with my biography, with my background. Thanks to all the jobs that I did in my life, I can say that I was very familiar with the system as it was back then. I had been to every local commune in Mostar, to all of the municipalities throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. I had visited all its most important enterprises. I was at the head, objectively speaking, of our social, economic transition. As someone who held office in the then Socialist Alliance, I was in a position to become familiar with all areas of life and the way in which social conflicts were overcome. I was familiar with the decision-making process, with the way health care and social welfare were organised, with retirement issues, youth and employment issues, import, export, monetary issues, defence-related issues, agriculture, the environment. While I was chairman of the executive council of the municipality, Mostar had just exceeded the magical figure of 50.000 employed. The potential for development was fantastic. I think this qualified me, relatively young as I was at the time, to become a member of the republican government. We launched our reforms immediately, and I was the sub-president in charge of the economy. As quickly as six months later, the last and most comprehensive programme of economic reform was launched. The reforms were more or less similar to those launched by all of the countries in Central and Eastern Europe, especially those that are today members of the European Union. The government grew in importance, and the party decreased in importance as did the Central Committee Of the League of Communists as the only party at the time. However, after the elections the parties grew in power again and the state mechanism was weakened as a result. In my opinion at least, this was the one fundamental reason for the bloody break-up of the former Yugoslavia that then ensued. In order to understand the overall context and bearing in mind the nature of the indictment, one must point out that in the former Yugoslavia there were three levels of government, constitutionally speaking: The federation, the republics, and the municipalities. All three of those were termed socio-political units or communities or states, if you like. The municipalities were not bodies of local government as they normally are in the countries of western democracy. They were more like states. They had indirect [Realtime transcript read in error "incorrect"] taxes, they had certain judicial functions, and they had their own internal affairs sector. In the briefest possible terms, the federal bodies were in charge of foreign policy, part of the judiciary, the relationships among the republics, defence, the currency, the exchange rates, customs-related issues, foreign trade, and military production in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. You can tell if you do not want to have this, but I see in the transcript on line 21 that you are quoted as saying that the municipalities had incorrect taxes. I'm pretty sure you did not say that but I seem to have understood indirect taxes. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] Indirect, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you mind if such corrections or question-- THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] No, no. Just go ahead. Thank you for your intervention. [Interpretation] The socialist republics and the same thing applied to the socialist republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina were on the whole responsible for public enterprises and for pensions. It was only in Bosnia and Herzegovina that there was a republican pension fund from which the money was paid to all the citizens. Also, responsible for taxes and for prices in the republic. The republican institutions financed the entire higher and primary education, the Ministry of the Interior, the building and maintaining of the major roads, water management, and, in part, culture, secondary education and the health care system, the judiciary system and various inspection services. The district TO staffs were part of the republican financing system while municipal staffs were bank rolled by municipalities. The health system was financed at the regional level as was, in part, secondary education. The chief regional institutions of Herzegovina, for example, in Mostar where the university -- the university, it was bank rolled by the -- a republican fund and the regional medical centre bank rolled by the regional health fund and partly by the republic itself. The municipalities were in charge of some of the general administrative issues, the cadaster, property-related issues, planning, social activities, social protection, public utilities such as garbage disposal, land-related issues, running towns, waterworks and sewage systems, some of the judiciary, and inspections in most of these areas. In 1990, we did some strengthening of the republican system. We started financing primary education because that was something that had to be done under the constitution, and the objective was to give all teachers the same sort of salary. As for internal affairs, municipalities bank rolled their own internal affairs, but they also paid their contributions into the regional fund, which led to a paradox. Salaries were smaller at these higher levels --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. You have now for the second time here used the term "regional." Could you explain what regional as opposed to federation, state, municipality, refers to, please? Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: There are three levels as I already told - Federation, republic, municipalities - but also intermediary institution was established inside republic. For instance, fund for finance of secondary education. Then before we took over all internal affairs, every municipality financed its own internal affairs, and contribution was proposed for every municipality to finance regional institution, and having in mind lack of financial discipline, some municipalities didn't provide money for that, and as the final effect we had the situation that regional chief and regional police had lower salaries than those in richer municipalities. It was the reason why we took over the whole internal affairs in 1990, just to provide unical system of police or internal affairs as we used to call that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: And please feel free to ask for any necessary explanation. [Interpretation] The objective was to create -- to create a more effective system of internal affairs to be maintained by the republican system and especially in those situations that turned out to be more complex as time was to show as soon as in 1991 the internal affairs system was ruptured at the seams by the separation of the Serb components, which soon led to the disintegration of the entire system. Our goal was to create a republic that would be economically strong, where the standards would be higher than those in the other republics. We wanted to stop being perceived as underdeveloped, and I think we were on the right track. The year is 1990. The Berlin Wall had just fallen. The reason we remember this year, because early that year there was a lot of optimism as far as the economy was concerned. There was a programme by the federal government as normally happens with this type of programme, the results at the outset were excellent and very promising. It had been prepared in secrecy, and I remember us preparing this programme in Belgrade in the last days of 1989. As a republic, we were prepared to carry a considerable burden because the prices of primary products were fixed and those were the dominant products in our -- in the structure of our economy such as, for example, the price of coal and the price of electricity. However, the Federal Executive Council and what was later to be the federal government or, rather, its president or chairman Ante Markovic buckled under the pressure exerted by Slobodan Milosevic for reasons that I believe to have been purely political. This was late in 1990, in March, and -- and he allowed the prices of energy sources to start soaring. As soon as one part of the programme was adjusted, without entering into all the political issues, I will deal mostly with economic issues, the whole thing began to be questioned, especially the fixed currency exchange rate. The issue of the economic disintegration, in my opinion, is another fundamental reason apart from other issues such as the never-resolved ethnic issues and other political issues. I believe our economy expert, the economy expert of my Defence team, will devote a lot of his time to talking about these issues. As far as the Executive Council of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, we were already committed to a European way at the time, and we were ahead of all the other socialist countries at the time. However, it was necessary to effect a number of the important changes. First of all, there needed to be a multi-party system. Secondly, there needed to be a liberalization of our economy, including privatisation of state-owned property. All of this under socially very difficult conditions. What we faced at the time, especially I, was a series of strikes that occurred in this period. The issue of property is something that is important to keep in mind in order, for example, to understand how socially-owned flats were used. Those were owned by a particular company, an enterprise, and a flat was then assigned to one of their workers. This is something we must bear in mind when we consider such problems as abandoned flats. There was unity in the Executive Council of Bosnia and Herzegovina. For example, the decision, because of the debt of the federation towards us, Bosnia and Herzegovina, as of October 1990, Bosnia should stop paying contributions into the federal fund was unanimously accepted. All of the Serb members of the Executive Council voted in favour of this decision, which we again ratified early in 1991 at a meeting that I chaired. This is Defence document 1D 02226. This was a clear measure to confirm that we were committed to the defence of the interest of the republic and its sovereignty vis-a-vis the dominant role of the federal authorities, but that was a message, too, to the other republics that we were committed to defending the interests of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is a rather well-known fact that the basic reason for the break-up of Yugoslavia was the emergence of the Serbian nationalism and the changes that Serbia introduced to restrict the routes of its autonomous provinces, Kosovo and Vojvodina, and the Republic of Montenegro, which was -- which had repercussions for the balance of the functioning of the federation causing the other republics and other ethnic groups to respond. I recall a meeting of the presidents of the governments of the republics and provinces with the Federal Executive Council in late 1990 where the economic policy measures for 1991 were debated. I interrupted the presentation by the Executive Council chairman Ante Markovic telling him that it didn't make any sense unless Serbia agreed to pay back the money, because it had already carried out the monetary coup. It literally stole from all of us several billions of dinars. That was possible in the monetary system of Yugoslavia as it was at the time. The other entities, not only the National Bank of Yugoslavia, could actually issue money. I reaffirmed this view before our council and also in public in early January 1991, again defending the economic interests of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is also in evidence. The Exhibit number is 1D 002232. In 1990 inflation and lack of trust came back, and the elections in the republics and the failure to call the elections at the federal level brought into question not only its functioning but also the operation of the unified economic area. Let me now say something briefly about the 1990 elections and the establishment of the new concept of power and government. When the law on citizens' associations was amended, new parties could be set up, but any attempts to organise on ethnic basis was prohibited. That was the position taken by the Executive Council, but we had to amend that because the Constitutional Court forced us to revise this decision. The members of the Trial Chamber can find this discussion, which is very interesting and which heralds the substance of the dispute concerning the constitutional order of the country, in document 1D 01615. It is important, because it shows the debate that -- before the constitutional court which is indicative of the essence of the conflict about the constitutional system in the country. Since according to the indictment the HDZ is part of the alleged joint criminal enterprise, it is interesting to note that in our view the HDZ was the loudest advocate of the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina, much more so than any other party. In its political platform, it stressed that it was, quote: “in favour of the mutual understanding and co-existence of Croats, Muslims, and Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina and other ethnic communities, and also in favour of Bosnia and Herzegovina joining the European Community”. The document is 1D 02699. At the elections in November 1990, the national parties won. They were all part of a coalition that aimed to fight against Communism, but in my view Communism had already defeated itself. Apart from the three national parties, the two parties that garnered the most votes were former Communist, the SDP, the reformists, a party led by Ante Markovic, the Federal Executive Council chairman. Those were parties that operated on the broader region -- in the broader region, not only Bosnia and Herzegovina. Yugoslavia still functioned at that time. I didn't want to take part in the elections. I did what I had announced I would do in early 1990. Those who were in power, in the light of their position and the fact that they had access to the media should not participate in the elections, but it was our task to create the most favourable conditions possible to ensure that after more than half a century the first elections could be as democratic and as free as possible. I wanted to go back to Mostar, because I had already been appointed the CEO of Apro Herzegovina. That's where my family lived, my relatives, and my wife's family. I would like to share my personal view with you. I believed that Yugoslavia could survive but on different -- on a different basis, but the Serbian political leadership did not like that. At the time when I was politically active, Yugoslavia was unlike the other socialist countries. There was freedom of movement. There was freedom of speech. Economic liberalism was growing. Since I was a member of a number of cabinets, almost 14 in my time, I can say that the deputies in the Assembly at that time were much more demanding than was the case after the multi-party system was introduced. We did the hand-over of the executive power to the new government, to Mr. Pelivan at the beginning of February 1991. I believe that Mr. Pelivan will appear in this court and to testify. But the new government did not rule in accordance with the rule of law but applying the principles of ethnic division, tripartite ethnic division in all the functions and at all levels. The result was a complete atrophy of the economic and political system. I will not be talking about the break-up of Yugoslavia. It's been dealt with before. The first war that resulted was the one in Slovenia, followed by the war in Croatia. I think that for the purpose of this trial it is enough to look at the minutes of the highest bodies of the HDZ of Bosnia and Herzegovina which are, by and large, part of the Prosecution evidence. The aggression on Croatia was condemned, aid organised. Volunteers are sent, Croats and Muslims alike. I was in Mostar. I was still the CEO of Apro Holding. I taught at the faculty, and I took part in drafting a number of studies related to the transformation of the economic system in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We had the whole of Yugoslavia as our market. We had two companies operating both in Zagreb and in Belgrade. The demands made at the HDZ meetings, you can see that from the minutes that were made public and were published by the media. So the demands are made to stop using the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina to launch attacks on Croatia. I cannot say whether this was done with the acquiescence of the people in the government, but the perception that existed among us citizens was that the Republic was not doing anything or was not doing enough to prevent the aggression against Croatia from the BiH territory. Bosnia and Herzegovina was no longer neutral. It became a participant in this war, all the more so because the Territorial Defence units from that republic participated in this war, those recruited from areas with a Serbian majority, of course. We can still hear the words of Alija Izetbegovic: "This is not our war." Regardless of the context in which this statement was made, it marked the tacit approval for Bosnia and Herzegovina to be used as a base to launch attacks on Croatia. As we heard in the testimony by Stjepan Kljuic in this courtroom, the transcript is at page 4017 and 4021, the ostensible neutrality of Izetbegovic in the war in Croatia was a position that was taken without consulting the legal organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina contrary to the constitutional obligations. As the president of this provisional government organisation the HVO, I couldn't make any decisions independently. I could only make decisions within the framework of this collective body. The same thing went for Izetbegovic or for anybody else who was part of this collective body. So these were all the topics that were discussed in the media at the time, and it was widely debated by all of us. Throughout this trial it is very important to take into account the context. For instance, Croats feared that an agreement would be reached by Serbs and Muslims. The war in Croatia had already affected areas with a Croatian majority, particularly in the western and north-western areas and in Ravno, a village in Herzegovina. When the JNA and the paramilitary forces launched an action, the forces that in September occupied Herzegovina and Mostar, I myself saw all that. The response of the authorities was very mild and not specific enough. The documents from the sessions of the BiH HDZ that I was not aware at the time except for the information that was published in the media, this was not something that I was aware of at the time when I was interviewed by the Prosecution, very clearly shows what the Croatian -- Croat politicians were doing at that time and how the Croatian communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina came to be established, eight of them with some 70 municipalities, which later united to form a single community, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The objectives were quite different to those that are being imputed in the indictment. Those minutes point the way as we tried to find an answer how those communities actually functioned. And here I would like to refer Your Honours to Prosecution Exhibits 41, 47, 50, 58, 60. The HDZ Presidency at its session of the 26th of August, quote: “denounces the using of the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the launching of terrorist attacks by the military and the volunteers against the Republic of Croatia”. Prosecution Exhibit P51. At the same time, the state organs in the republic is slowly ceasing to function. The divisions, the rifts become ever deeper. By mid-1991, the representatives of the government in Sarajevo admit in their public statements that they no longer control the situation in the whole territory. This was a fact that was general knowledge. I'm presenting this because the Prosecution has failed to show the context that would make it possible to understand what is actually going on. The picture that was presented in Mr. Tomljanovich’s so called expert report was especially biased and totally one-sided. I am aware, Your Honours, that you do not want to dwell on details from the past and you're right, but we have to follow the injunction by historian Huising that we have to view all the events and all the statements in order to be able to see what options were available at any given time. This is the only correct approach that this Chamber should adopt in evaluating all the evidence, including the presidential transcripts that I will now very briefly mention. Together with other members of the delegation, I participated, of course, at a certain number of talks with President Tudjman, once in 1992 in September, twice in 1993 in November. For the most part those meetings took place after the period relevant for the indictment. I was not aware of the fact those talks were being taped. There are, of course, parts of those conversations that are inaccurate. In some cases the speakers are misidentified or are not identified at all. Those transcripts make interesting reading for historians, of course, but also for anyone who wants to study the context. Tudjman was a historian, and he wanted to keep a record of everything he was doing and everything he was talking about. Opinions as to the method he applied differ. We now have excerpts from those conversations in front of us, before the court, a criminal court. For the Prosecution, they prove that there was a joint criminal enterprise. As far as my defence is concerned, they prove that there was no joint criminal enterprise, not even a hint of one. Transcripts cannot be used from the position of hindsight and in attempt to fit them into some kind of narrative or by performing selective cut and paste. We have to look at them in the context of at least two elements, the situation in the field at the time and the international negotiations that were going on at the time. In its decision on motion under Rule 98 bis, the Chamber mentions that it is said in P6454, dated the 5th of November, 1993, that Mostar had all assets to be the capital city of Herceg-Bosna. Well, this was envisaged by the international plan about the union of the three republics that was being negotiated under the auspices of the UN and the European Community. The last witness in the Prosecution case brought with him documents indicating that the Muslim side accepted Mostar as the capital of Herceg-Bosna, one of the three republics in the union of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Tudjman was aware, or at least this is what we can see from the transcripts, that the international community would play the decisive role in this crisis. He was also aware of the fact that the basic factors in the crisis -- generating the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina were Serbs and Muslims, not Croats, and that is why maintaining their position as the population with the smallest number was the most complex one. The transcripts show several constant elements. Even when the attacks of the BH army on Croats and the HVO were at their fiercest, Tudjman still advocated full cooperation with the Muslims. He also signed a secret agreement with Izetbegovic on confederation, but only two days later, on the 16th of September, 1993, Izetbegovic in turn signs an agreement with the Serbs allowing them to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina with their own republic two years later, provided that the Muslim republic gains [Realtime transcript read in error "against"] the international recognition in accordance with the proposal of the Republic of Bosnia that this Chamber had an opportunity to see in the course of this trial. In reading all the transcripts, I could see that the constant element in Tudjman's talks was to stop the war at any cost. The defence of the fundamental rights of Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina is a following element which is a constant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. Since your statement is of course for me at least a very important one, I would like to say that there is an important mistake in the transcript in -- in page -- sorry, 15, I believe, that it says that the -- provided that the Muslim republic against the international recognition. You said that the Muslim republic gains the international recognition in accordance with the proposal of the Republic of Bosnia, et cetera. So I would like to make a comment here that since you -- you would like to finish, of course, in time, you are talking a bit quickly, and it is important that the transcript should be a correct one, and therefore I would advise you to slow down a bit for -- for the translation. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: Thank you, Judge Prandler, for the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the speaker, please. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: I said that those agreement allow Serbian Republic to live and that in national recognition would remain on Muslim republic or Bosnia republic. This document was introduced before this case. Thank you. [Interpretation] The Defence of the fundamental rights of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina was the next element, and most convincingly, the most important element that pervades -- pervaded all of the conversations was to ensure the territorial and legal sovereignty of Croatia within the internationally-recognised borders and obviously the protection of these borders. Until, in 1994, the Joint Command of the HVO and the BiH army took off the ground, and in cooperation with the modernised Croatian army, conditions were put in place for the Dayton Accords to be signed once the largest part of Bosnia and Herzegovina was freed, and I witnessed those events as the minister of defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. These are my impressions after having read all the transcripts, and I'm sure that the Defence witnesses, including Miomir Zuzul and Mile Akmadzic, Prime Minister of the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, will certainly speak about these transcripts. In an interview which is the Prosecution Exhibit 9078, I said that an important number of both Croats and Muslims in Herzegovina emotionally was in favour of joining these parts to -- with Croatia after Yugoslavia was dissolved. The opinions of Croats have not changed in the meantime according to many polls. The state border, which was just established by Herceg-Bosna, divided members of the same people who had spent more than a century living in the same state. In the meantime, the differences in the standard of living became deeper after the dissolution of Yugoslavia, bearing in mind the higher level of economic development of the Republic of Croatia. The events and the developments in the first half of 1992 completely skipped in the Prosecution case. One should say only briefly that Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised as an independent state owing to primarily the support of the HDZ to Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croats in that state. The available documentation points to the fact that the international community basically had two pre-conditions in order to recognise Bosnia and Herzegovina. The first one was to the hold a referendum which was requested by Badinter's commission. Another condition was an agreement on the internal regulation of a relationship within Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is proved, for example, by a joint American and European Community declaration on the recognition of Yugoslav republics dated 10 March 1992. This Trial Chamber is already familiar with the statement on the principle of the constitutional organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina dated 18 March, which was adopted by the three sides or the three peoples living in the state. The witnesses will speak about these principles, i.e., they will say that constitutional units have the right, and I quote: "To pass regulations and manage the issues of importance for constitutional units such as the administration of services and officers of these units, the expropriation of property for public use, the cadaster, the protection from fire, Chambers of commerce, companies, savings houses and credit institutions. Furthermore, social protection, education, police, trade." Every constitutional unit has the right to maintain relationships with others and organise their own institutions. That is why a series of negotiations took place under the auspices of the European Community, and the Portuguese diplomat Jose Cutileiro was engaged all with a view to arriving at a mutually-adopted principles of the future organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina before the formal recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina. What I'm saying is this: Since I was a member of the government prior to these events, that in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the former Yugoslavia there was no single element that would protect the rights of different peoples, because that part of the care was in the hands of the Communist Party, and it was the Communist Party that guaranteed the rights to all the different peoples, and not some explicit articles of the Constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This information that those were two pre-conditions for recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina is corroborated by documents, by witness statements, as well as my information that I had at the time and the contacts that I had in the United States of America at the time. All the proposals of constitutional solutions for Bosnia and Herzegovina proposed during international conferences started from the qualification of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a union of peoples. Within the context of peace talks, let me just announce my defence will deal with the issue of the alleged agreement in Graz, the issue of the Serb and Croat division of Bosnia and Herzegovina that this Trial Chamber mentions in the decision pursuant to Rule 98 bis, transcript page 28215. The witnesses and the evidence will show that this meeting was held on the recommendation of international mediators. Nothing was agreed at that meeting. On the contrary, the Croatian side made an offer whereby all the sticking issues would be resolved by an international arbitration. A similar meeting was held between Croats and Muslims within the same week in Split. In addition to numerous newspaper articles, I will also present evidence Prosecution number 9526 and 1D 00525. I'm using the word "Muslims" rather than the word "Bosniaks," because the word "Bosniak" was adopted only when the Constitution of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina was adopted in March 1994, so when using the word "Muslim" I am not implying anything. I'm just trying to put things straight historically. The available documentation shows that both Croatian communities that were established, both Herceg-Bosna and Bosnian Posavina in November 1991, were dormant, were not active until the general attack of the JNA and the Serb formations in March and particularly at the beginning of April 1992 after the international recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The decision on the establishment of the Croatian Defence Council as a defence army was passed on the 8th of April 1992. At that time, as Mr. Tomljanovich, a member of the OTP, there was no army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is page 6818 of the transcript. Mate Boban signed this decision as the president of the HVO and the HZ HB. He himself explained to the general public the reasons why the army had been established, and he emphasised that the process leading to the establishment of the Crisis Staffs in the municipalities and their regional linking had led to the establishment of the HVO staff. Talking about the relationship with the other armed forces that were defending the country, he said, "We expect the continuation of the negotiations on the constitutional order of the -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the moment when we're sure that the constitutional order as envisaged by the general principles on -- of the conference of BiH will become a fact, that's when we can start negotiation -- negotiations with the other forces in BH." This is P 157. In his book, the Prosecution witness Cupina on page 460 says that before the HVO was established Boban -- Boban had proposed in Sarajevo that a decision should be reached about the establishment of the Croatian-Muslim or Muslim-Croatian Defence council. Obviously, this was not accepted by the Sarajevo authorities, and these authorities as we have heard from Stjepan Kljuic, the Commander-in-Chief of the BH army, admitted themselves that they could not do much about the defence of the state. Before the formal establishment of the HVO as an army on the 8th of April,across Bosnia and Herzegovina a network of smaller or bigger units had been established, and these units had already been engaged in defence activities. Obviously I did not have that information at the time. The establishment of the first military to defend Bosnia and Herzegovina, in paragraph 25 of this indictment is defined by the Prosecution as part of the joint criminal enterprise. A military which was an integral part of the armed forces of the country, the members of which enjoyed exactly the same status as the members of the other component of the armed forces of BiH, in the free territory of that state. They enjoy to this day the same benefits and receive the same remuneration from the same state as invalids, as decorated individuals, and they enjoyed the same rights in the privatisation of socially-owned assets. If you follow the context of the establishment of the Croatian Community and the Presidency as its principle body of administration, then one can see that eight months after the establishment one can notice a change in the decision on the establishment that was included on the 3rd of July, 1992. The Presidency became the legislative body of the HZ HB and incorporated members such as the municipal presidents of the HVO, and I could witness that at the session on the 14th of August. When I looked at that decision, and not only that one but also others that were published in Official Gazettes number 1 and 2, my first impression was rather disappointing, primarily with regard to their legal quality and regulation as a whole. To be honest, these -- this was more an improvisation than an announcement of a more serious enterprise. The Amended Decision on Establishment, in the amended Article 8, envisaged that the Presidency would establish the executive and administrative bodies of government. We cannot look at that without any context what actually happened within the eight months leading to that period. What happened was this: First of all, war in Croatia was at a standstill. Second of all, there was no clear outline as to the future organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Third of all, there had been a series of talks under the auspices of the European Community, and the principles were adopted from Cutileiro's plan dated 18 March about the future organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Fourthly, Bosnia and Herzegovina, owing to the support of Croats and the HDZ, had been recognised internationally after the referendum. Fifthly, the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina was waging in all parts of the country, and as was pointed out in the decision on martial law which was passed on the 20th of June, 1992, by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, by that time 70 per cent of the territory had been occupied by the Serbs and the non-Serb population had been expelled. Sixthly, the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had been dissolved after it met for the last time on the 25th of January when a decision was passed to hold the referendum, and the government of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was no longer functioning, and it did not have any influence outside Sarajevo or virtually no influence because Sarajevo was completely encircled, and several witnesses have already spoken about that. Seventh, municipalities adopted a majority of the functions of the former Yugoslav Federation and Republican government, which imposed a need to coordinate their activities, and I will speak about that briefly in -- later. HVO had already defended significant parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina where they had been established; for example, in Herzegovina, Central Bosnia, and Posavina. And the ninth thing that I would like to mention, there was a more pronounced lack of willingness to give the HVO an equal status as an armed formation in the defense of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The witnesses and evidence will speak about that. The very independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina required an enormous effort in terms of passing new regulations and taking over the functions formerly held by Yugoslavia. Since this actually never happened apart from a formal hand-over in terms of certain laws simply because the administration at the time did not allow for anything like that to be adopted, the entire system simply collapsed in all its key features. This particularly applies to the financial system. There was a shortage of currency in the country's economy. As soon as April, bills stopped being paid, especially those that used to be covered by republican funds. I am a witness to the fact that the Community of Herceg-Bosna never adopted a formal constitution severing its links with Bosnia and Herzegovina. It never adopted a statute to begin with which would have been a precondition for registering with a court any form of citizens' association, hunters, bird-watchers, music lovers, what have you. It respected sovereignty in all its documents. Whenever the name was used, HZ HB, we would always highlight the name of the state of which it was a part, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. What I'm trying to say it this, and this might be the key message of this introduction, is that the implementation and preservation of the constitutional order of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not go down the chain of the state authorities because that never actually worked. Rather, it was a grassroots phenomenon. The existing communal system was strengthened and so were the institutions and powers of certain municipalities that were part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the objective being to meet the constitutional obligations of each and every citizen and each and every municipality across the country, this being the defence of the country. In the summer of 1992, when the municipalities took over most of the attributes of the state, there was a need for coordination in their work. That's what we were told at the time, and that, too, was my interpretation. This led to the establishment of a provisional organ of executive government. I will try to briefly explain what it was like, how it worked, who the members were, what it succeeded in doing at least in part, what it was responsible for, and what it was not responsible for. The first statutory decision on the setting up of the executive was adopted on the 15th of May. However, it took over a year to organise and properly set up this body, and this is shown by the decision on the nomination and establishment published by the Official Gazette. In the documentation submitted by the OTP, there are numerous copies of this statutory decision of the 15th of May, but the OTP omitted to tender into evidence one of them with an article which reads, and I quote: "The president of the HZ HB is the president of the HVO." The ERN number for this document is 006889378938. In the indictment, the Prosecutor defines the HVO as the one major defence body and body of the executive, although these are two entirely different bodies and terms. Even the most perfunctory look at both of these statutory decisions. The 15th of May one and the 3rd of July one - defines the HVO as, quote: “the body of executive government and administration throughout the HZ HB”, which at the very outset tells us this is an entirely new body in relation to the HVO as an armed force, and this is something that I had mentioned when speaking about the decision to set up the army dated the 8th of April, 1992. The statutory decision tells us that the HVO of the HZ HB is a provisional body which will continue to perform its function until proper executive authorities are set up, which leaves perfectly clear that this was a provisional body. It also tells us that members of the HVO, this provisional organ of executive government, were jointly responsible for any decisions taken by the Croatian Defence Council, and each of those members are personally responsible for their own areas of work. This was, after all, the conclusion drawn also by Professor Ribicic at 14333 of the transcript in the Blaskic case. [In English] "The HVO as a whole and every individual member of the HVO accountable for the work to the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." [Interpretation] The taking over of certain functions was a matter of necessity. This was needed in order to overcome the growing chaos. The links to the existing government in Sarajevo were essential. It was precisely the representatives of the HDZ in that government, that is, the party that had set up the HZ HB, who lent the minimum legitimacy to those organs, and that sort of legitimacy was necessary for Bosnia and Herzegovina to be able to continue to function as internationally- recognised subjects to begin with. The first statutory decision actually creates the office of the president of the HZ HB and the HVO with heads of departments. The president remains the president of the Presidency of the HZ HB. He's in charge of the army and the executive. He signs all decisions in his capacity as the president of the HZ HB and the president of the HVO. Furthermore, it is necessary to point out that this concentration of power at the level of the Presidency of the HZ HB, a body where the mayors of all the municipalities that are represented, the basic intention was to stay within the bounds of the constitution of the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was no division of power which, after all, was typical of the entire Yugoslav system based, as it was, on the unity of power. Here, we encounter a rudimentary form of power, and we cannot talk of division but rather of distribution of the purported power. The system being what it was and being as provisional as it was, the Presidency of the HZ HB was the legislative body, and the HVO was a provisional body of the civilian government which on the 14th of August, 1992, in an operational sense became the civilian executive body. The Presidency of the HZ HB is at the apex. Power streams down from them to the municipalities, which then coordinate all joint activities. A link is thus established between the Departments and the Presidency where presidents of the municipal HVO branches are represented. That is my understanding of these documents, documents that were poor from a legal standpoint, yet they are useful for us to describe how the bodies actually worked in reality. One thing that is not defined, for example, are the tasks and powers of this provisional executive organ, the HVO, which had been the case before with the executive boards of the municipal assemblies or, rather, the Executive Board of Bosnia and Herzegovina's Assembly. At the close of my presentation, I will be addressing documents adopted by the Presidency, by the HVO, the HZ HB, in the light of paragraph 17 of the indictment. However, it is important to point out as early as now that the legislation -- a look at the legislation at the very outset tells us that only minimal changes were introduced of the existing republican legislation, and this was needed for the regulations to be applied at all. All this legislation containing thousands of laws continue to apply. Changes were only introduced to some of those because that was the only way they could have made sense. For example, this was necessary in order to have the criminal provisions in a situation where there was no domestic currency and none to be used. The Presidency then adopted a decision to set up public enterprises, public companies as early as July 1992, but they weren't set up before later on. The railway system and the roads in 1993, the radio in March 1993. If we read the indictment, we see that the Presidency of the HZ HB made two decisions on taking over JNA and SSNO property, SSNO meaning Federal Secretariat for All People's Defence. Prior to those decisions, however, most of the municipalities had adopted these very same decisions. Talking of property and particularly various views on how abandoned flats were to be used, a particular example of discrimination in this field would be the way this was dealt with by the Republican government. Jablanica municipality, for example, seized not just the money of the occupiers but also of all the users from municipal territory. The JNA facilities were taken over by Tuzla municipality, the JNA flats by Travnik municipality and Mostar municipality. Three months after this same decision adopted, as well, by its own municipal president, Livno took the same decision to seize and requisition the property of the occupying force for municipal purposes. It is quite obvious that the municipalities had the -- the requisite power, and the decision taken by the HZ HB was an attempt to coordinate. Now for a brief digression about my job back in 1992, having been appointed president of the HVO HZ HB on the 14th of August. When the war in Croatia broke out, we who were working in the economy were facing increasing problems. Road traffic was being disrupted, and the situation was becoming more and more difficult. I didn't know most of the people in the HDZ at the time, but I tried to stay in touch with people in the republican government. This was, after all, part of my job as the CO of a corporation with 14 joint stock companies and about 4.000 employees. I do believe that the Honourable Chamber will be receiving documentation on the company that I was running at the time. As I had announced -- as I have announced already, 1990, my commitment was to an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. Early 1992, I said this loud and clear in a special TV show on TV Sarajevo, “I Want to Say”. This is 1D 02074. It's part of the evidence in this case already. The position that I put forward at the time was crystal clear. In order to survive, Bosnia and Herzegovina must be both as near as possible and as far as possible from Serbia and Croatia and must try to have symmetric relations with these two. I had a historic opportunity eight years later after a series of interstate agreements with Croatia to endorse this with my own signature in Belgrade. This was about the diplomatic relations between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia, and this finally re-established this new order in our part of the world. Jure Pelivan, who was prime minister at the time and I believe is due to appear in this courtroom, asked me to allow him to propose me for appointment as the governor of the National Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Early in 1992 I accepted this, but only on a provisional basis and only in order to be the one to issue the first currency ever used in this new Bosnia and Herzegovina. It had become clear to me that without being successful in protecting our sovereignty in terms of our currency, any other objective in terms of our economy would have been lost. Even before my appointment passed the procedure in the Assembly, I saw the need to act urgently. Therefore, I embarked on this project as soon as possible. I even made a visit to Croatia's national bank in order to familiarise myself with the procedures that they used when they first -- first started issuing their own money. I can say that I had the project ready. I had talked to people from the Personnel Commission of the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of BH. However, Muharem Cero, the chairman of that commission told me just before the vote in the Assembly told me that a telegram had arrived that the consensus to go ahead with my appointment had be withdrawn. I was to learn later on that someone back in Mostar's HDZ was not happy with my appointment. The currency was never issued and as the months to follow were to show, the whole economic system collapsed.
