utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing's resumed. Mr. Prlic, you have the floor. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. In early March, after the referendum was held and without having any inkling that the situation could escalate, I went to the USA. I was invited by the American government through Ambassador Warren Zimmermann to participate in a study trip. The theme was market economy, US approach. That's where I met the first US ambassador to BiH. I came back from the USA and stepped right into the war. I could have stayed there. I might have been an expert in a trial similar to this one had I stayed in Washington, but my place was in my country, in my town. I came to Mostar after a couple of days, sometime around the 10th of April, 1992, after a long trip by way of Belgrade where I landed from New York together with the football players of Velez, a Mostar club, who played their last Premiership game in Yugoslavia as it existed at the time, in Subotica. I approached Mostar from the eastern side and I saw the cannon batteries shelling Mostar. My family had already left town and my eldest daughter stopped attending school. The school was no longer opened. I tried to salvage at least some of the production lines in the holding companies. Mostar was completely besieged and it was shelled all the time. I was a member of the Municipal Territorial Defence Staff before the war. That was my wartime assignment. All conscripts had those assignments. I reported on duty, but it did not function. The Territorial Defence itself broke down as had all other state institutions. Neven Tomic put me in contact with the HVO. The HVO had already set up its units. I became a volunteer. I was issued a uniform and a rifle. We were committed to defending the town where I had gone through everything. This is where I went to school. This is where I fell in love. This is where I had my friends, my family, my job, my university. I really appreciated and was thankful to the people who had realised that there would be war and who had prepared for it. I didn't know that that would come to pass. Somebody bought, gave money for this uniform and this rifle. The uniforms and the rifles that we paid by making contributions from our salaries were now in the possession of the JNA that had positions in the hills around the town. After that, as a member of the HVO, of the military, I was appointed to the council for special purposes. That was Puljic [Realtime transcript read in error, "Pusic"] and Tomic's idea. It was a group of younger people mostly with a business background, managers from well-known companies who wanted to use the means that still remained in those companies and to put their business connections outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina to some use, to help mount a defence and to organise life. It was obvious that there was no executive government in the town, and all of us expected that once the government was set up we had great expectations from this government. The government was set up by the two parties that had won in the elections, the SDA and the HDZ. Things did improve. The new authorities wanted us to submit reports. I submitted one such report in June when the HVO liberated Mostar about the situation in the Apro Herzegovina companies. The document number is 1D 02390. At that time, nobody received any salaries. We heard that some remuneration was handed out in some municipalities, in particular to soldiers. Check-points were set up at the borders of municipalities. In addition to controlling passengers, transport of goods was also controlled and municipal duties were paid directly. The most accurate characterisation would be that every municipality assume the functions from the other levels of government that existed in the former Yugoslavia, the federation and the republics, and this resulted in an even greater chaos. There was this need to coordinate their work because the government in Sarajevo simply did not have any influence over what was going on in the field. This was confirmed through my contacts with the people I knew who were in the government. Sometime up until mid-May it was still possible to remain in telephone contact with Sarajevo. The agreement on the friendship and cooperation between Bosnia and Croatia dated the 21st of July, which was widely publicised, meant that there were no controversial issues between Muslims and Croats. That's the way I and my friends understood it. The HVO was accepted as an armed force on an equal footing, and the civilian authorities were supposed to be brought in line with the internal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in accordance with the basic concept of the three constituent units. That's Prosecution Exhibit P 339. As I explained in my interview, at the second meeting with Boban in the summer of 1992, and I have to note here that I had not known Boban before the war, I was offered to do the thing that it was thought I could do best, where I could make the biggest contribution, to try and set up some kind of coordination with the municipalities and the government of the republic in order to prevent the growing chaos in the organisation of the civilian life in the society. After thinking about it for a long time, I accepted this task to assist in coordinating certain measures to be taken by the municipalities in order to establish the unified economic area. Each and every patriot would do the same. We were brought up in the system of All Peoples Defence where everybody was supposed to make their contribution within one's abilities. Legally, this obligation applied to everyone between the ages of 16 and 60, but even younger people were supposed to contribute, even as a young boy, not yet 10, and later as a boy scout. We were all brought up with the idea that we should do that to defend our country. Boban was quite clear. He told me, "Do whatever you can do in the civilian area," but as I've pointed out in the interview, he said, "You have nothing to do with the military and the police." And he kept his word. In the Official Gazette and in the minutes from the session of the HZ HB Presidency of the 14th of August, my appointment as the head of the finance department is mentioned. The date is the 15th of May, 1992. As I said in the interview, I was told about that immediately before the session, the session where I was appointed the presidents -- the president, so that I never did perform this function at all. There are Defence exhibits that will prove that, but generally speaking, when I assume a post I tend to leave my mark. So from the 14th of August onwards, it is possible to follow how the provisional organ of executive government functioned and what my role was. The nature and the contents of the HVO HZ HB that I described as provisional in my interview to the Prosecution, and noting that it operated within the framework of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was defined by certain documents, and I suggest that the Trial Chamber consult them, the statutory decision on the provisional structure of the executive government and administration. That's a document of the 3rd of July. The amendments of the 17th of October are contained in document P 00684, and special emphasis should be placed on Articles 20 and 22. The second is the decree on the structuring and purview of departments and commissions. That's Exhibit 1D 00001, Articles 3 through 7 and 33. The third is the Rules Of Procedure of the HVO HZ HB, Prosecution Exhibit P 09539, and in particular, the work as reflected in the minutes of the sessions of the HVO HZ HB, they have all been admitted into evidence as Prosecution exhibits, although unfortunately no witness was called to actually talk about them. The fifth reference are issues of the Official Gazette of the HZ HB which show in a completely transparent manner what HVO HZ HB actually did but also what it did not do. I would like to say first of all that this organ was a collective organ. It was set up eight months after my appointment, cannot be considered a cabinet, contrary to what Prosecution team member Tomljanovich persistently claimed. In our area the term "government" does not appear before the 90s. Before that you had executive bodies, Executive Boards in the municipalities, Executive Councils in the Republics, but the Assembly was always the key organ because there was unity of power. The term "prime minister" appears for the first time in the federation constitution of 1994. This constitution was drafted under the US auspices. So in our region we had never had a political system that would be based on the role of the prime minister such as, for instance, is the case in the United Kingdom, so that this constant stressing of the term "prime minister" does not have any basis, either formally or in any kind of essence. The body that I was a member of did its work in sessions and this was based on the rules of -- Rules of Procedure. This was based on the statutory decision on the provisional structure of the executive government. In Article 16 it is stated: "The HVO shall operate in sessions." And in paragraph 4 of the same article it is indicated that the HVO shall determine in greater detail its internal structure and other issues in its Rules of Procedure. So the only form in which HVO HZ HB was active was by having those sessions. This is why the preparation of the material envisaged for sessions’ agendas, as well as the decision- making process, were regulated in detail. Defence witnesses will show that this manner of functioning of the executive organs in the administration organs was actually taken over from the existing system of state administration in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and municipalities operated according to the same principle, for instance, Tuzla, Siroki Brijeg, or the Executive Board of the Mostar municipality while I was president in 1988. We will be tendering those documents. The fact that this was a typical document of this kind, Rules of Procedure regulating the work of a collective organ is confirmed by the Rules of Procedure on the work of the Presidency of the HZ HB, which is identical in the way it regulates the work mutatis mutandis. Of course the word HVO -- the acronym HVO is replaced by the Presidency of the HZ HB and the bodies of the HVO become members of the HZ HB Presidency. Speaking about the Rules of Procedure I would like to add that the provisional organ of the executive government never set up its work programme which would be obligatory for its departments and sub-departments. Only obligations towards the collective organ were determined on an ongoing basis. The bodies had their own independent programmes, in accordance with their competencies. So a document that would be entitled, The Programme of Activities of the HVO HZ HB does not exist. We did not pass such a document because for the most part we merely responded to situations. We didn't manage them. The first work programme was drafted by the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. It was adopted by the House of Representatives of the HR HB for 1994, and this is a completely different topic. The role of the president in the executive government organ is identical to that of any president in any collective organ including the parliament. This person is supposed to prepare and chair the sessions, has only one vote, as do all the other members. In urgent cases decisions can be made on the basis of individual opinions stated by HVO members without them being discussed at the session, but at the first following session the contents of the decision are adopted for the record. This is Article 26. The documents that are published in Official Gazette indicate that in the initial period Mate Boban did have the sovereign right and did pass regulations and other documents even when there was no clear legal basis signing the decrees as "the president," the president of the HZ HB or both, the president of the HVO and the HZ HB. It arises from these short remarks, first of all, the HVO as an armed force was established on the 8th of April, 1992. Its mission was clear, and I quote: "To look after the defence of the Croatian people as well as of all the other peoples in the community when they come under attack by anybody," which points to the fact that this was exclusively a military organisation. The second HVO, which was charged with executive power by a statutory decision issued on the 15th of May was a formally new body, and that's why I quote the HVO is established, is used. At that time the HVO was both the executive and administrative power of the HZ HB with original authority and the pronounced powers of the president, and this HVO existed up to the 14th of August, 1992. And the third one, after the 14th of August, 1992, the HVO HZ HB lost some of its powers and competencies and there was no significant influence of the president. We can arrive at this conclusion if we compare the original statutory decision on the interim organisation of power and the subsequent amendments and supplements in Article 18 as well as with the corresponding provisions of the Rules of Procedure of the HVO and other fundamental documents that were issued after the 14th of August, 1992. This Trial Chamber has been informed that by amending the Statutory decision a possibility was given to the provisional organ of executive government to adopt documents from the purview of the Presidency of the HZ HB in situations that did not allow for procrastination. This is the usual practice whereby the Parliament authorises the executive organ to adopt documents from its competences under circumstances of war or emergency situations, but that body, at the following session of the legislative organ had to have those decisions confirmed, and this is something that Professor Ribicic has spoken about before this Trial Chamber. Obviously, all the decisions that were based on the aforementioned authority and which were passed pursuant to that authority were actually the decisions of the Presidency of the HZ HB. Now this is about de jure, and now on to the de facto. After the meeting of the 14th of August, the newly appointed head of the finance department and I returned to Mostar in my car that was later on seized by a brigade. We did not have any room to work in. We did not have any equipment. We did not have any staff, and we did not have any clear guidelines to govern us in our activity. We sat ourselves down at two computers and we started preparing and drafting financial regulations based on the previous legislation of Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and the municipal scope of authority. At that moment I believe that this was the most important activity that might help us to overcome the chaos that ruled at the time. The most important source of income at the time when the economy had stopped functioning were the donations of our citizens who worked abroad. Through their municipalities they funded defence. Every municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina had a decision that regulated those donations. That's why we prepared documents to regulate those donations and to channel them for the armed forces of Herceg-Bosna. We thought that this was only logical. We did not want these funds to be dissipated across various municipalities. For example, rich municipalities which were not on the front lines would give salaries to their soldiers, whereas the municipalities who did not have foreign workers and which were located on the front line, such as Mostar or Stolac, or perhaps municipalities in Central Bosnia, could not give their soldiers anything. They could not provide for them. However, when we prepared the -- this regulation, the municipalities that had significant income rebelled against that regulation. Boban called me and asked me to withdraw that document. We adopted it only in March 1993, but again all the funds were sent to the municipalities. They did not go to Herceg-Bosna. The only thing that we managed to define was to have the same amount for everybody who worked abroad and who wanted to give donations. At the very outset I realised what would be the difficulties that we would face in an attempt to coordinate even the most obvious or most trivial things, and this is what showed me what I would have to do to reach a win-win strategy. We adopted a standard routine of work in sessions as had been envisaged. Maybe I should say -- add to that there were no sessions with secret documents. There were no secret documents which I believe is interesting bearing in mind that we had to work under war conditions. The provisional organ of executive government tried to regulate issues in a growing number of areas in order to prevent the escalation of chaos, which de jure means that the competencies of the provisional body of executive government were not defined from the outset in the regulations which have been mentioned. Instead of that, the situation always imposed new issues that had to be dealt with and regulated. Initiatives arrived from various institutions that those issues should be regulated. For example, from the institution for education, from the automotive clubs and similar situations. The minutes which served as Prosecutor's exhibits testified to the way we worked. For example, at the 7th session that was held on the 14th October 1992, my words were recorded – “An analysis of the work of the HVO HZ HB shows that during these two months, i.e., from the day of its establishment, a lot has been regulated but not very much has been implemented.” The break- up of Yugoslavia and interruption of all the telecommunication traffic and other links with the republican bodies and the self-organisation with a view to defending the state from aggression over the past period the municipalities had taken over the role of the state, especially in financial terms. That is why today we're faced with some instances in which the municipalities behave as the state. I am cutting short the quotation. It is necessary to appoint people regardless of their ethnic background, be it a Muslim or a Croat, and when they're appointed it should be pointed out that their appointment is temporary. People who arrive from the municipalities will have food and lodgings provided for in the pensioners' home where my office was located at the time. This is Prosecution Exhibit P 578. I knew that the municipalities were independent in the previous system as well, but I could not even imagine that the activities were so developed until the moment when we were able to obtain the Official Gazettes of a significant number of municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina which showed that the municipalities would proclaim the aggressor, that they would engage in a mobilisation of people much earlier than the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina had done that. They organised public companies in the areas of telecommunication and electricity supply. They had taken over the revenues of Yugoslavia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. They introduced new currencies. They had taken over authority of banks and the financial institutions. They also established bodies and appointed people in the judiciary. They defined the rights of movement of people, the reception, accommodation and status of displaced persons, and so on and so forth. For example, all the municipalities had adopted decisions on a ban to receive refugees. We would have tens of decisions about all this, both from Croatian majority municipalities and from municipalities with a Muslim majority such as Mostar, Capljina, Tuzla, Maglaj, Jablanica, Siroki Brijeg, Posusje, Gornji Vakuf, Uskoplje, Livno, Posusje, Orasje, the entire free territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I'm talking about the areas that were not occupied by the JNA, i.e., the Serb army. Your Honours, a question may be raised at this moment as to whether by introducing these measures the municipalities had violated the constitution, especially bearing in mind that it was about -- that those decisions were about their defence. Formally speaking, they all did, without exception. But the constitutional obligation of the municipalities and the spirit of the constitution was to organise the defence, and you have to bear that in mind. That was the objective that all the municipalities had in mind, and their intentions were good. They improvised. They were not consistent in passing their decisions, but the municipalities that had organised their defence and that had undertaken other measures had actually complied with their constitutional obligation to defend their country, those municipalities that didn't do anything and waited for somebody else to do that, for example, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that had actually attacked Bosnia and Herzegovina, or that they -- or that had waited for the measures of the central government which only on the 20th of June, 1992, proclaimed martial law did not comply with their constitutional obligation. This was just an expression of the implementation of the approach of All People’s Defence which was deeply enrooted in the tradition of my people. One of the presidential transcript speaks about a reception on the occasion of 125th anniversary of Home Guards Movement. The All Peoples Defence was a system in which every citizen, every institution -- I hope that Mr. -- Judge Trechsel will not hold it against me if I say that this was very similar to the system in Switzerland, was obliged to defend their country, and nobody, nobody had the right to sign defeat. And under the law, everybody was duty-bound to prepare defence plans, but this time the aggressor was not a NATO or a Warsaw Pact country, and this had been what -- the thing that we had prepared for. It was actually the army that was supposed to defend the country from the outside aggressor. However, regardless of the success of the municipalities in taking over the functions of the state, new chaos was created. The municipalities on the front line had more problems and less funds to deal with those problems. Check-points were established. There was no tender. There was no tender. There was no payment system, and this was the main problem that I had to deal with in professional terms, to put it that way. No modern society can be organised if a payment system is not in place. Without payment transactions, there is no normal life. In order for the system to function, for example, if, for example, the members of the Trial Chamber wanted to use their credit card for any transaction, several pre-conditions have to be set in place. First, there has to be tender; B, there has to be a bank where your account is held; and C, the telecommunication system has to function in order to implement your order or your payment transaction. None of these elements in Bosnia and Herzegovina functioned at the time. There was nothing. And now before I start talking about particular areas, let me say something about my first encounter with President Tudjman, which happened on the 17th of September, 1992. Document number is 1D 02366, and this is a transcript that has been fully translated at the request of my Defence. The transcript points to the complexity of this situation at the time, and reading the transcript you can see that the Croatian leadership was committed to defending Bosnia and Herzegovina and building Bosnia and Herzegovina as a modern state that would take into account the interests of all the three constituent peoples. Also, there was a commitment to achieve peace in the shortest possible period of time in keeping with the propositions of the London conference. During that encounter, I spoke about the goals of organising civilian authorities. I mentioned the publication of the Official Gazette that just appeared --

I'm now looking at the documents, and I can't find that particular document. Is there a mistake somewhere? THE ACCUSED PRLIC: I suppose it is mistake, because I don't think that you make mistake, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because your meeting with President Tudjman is indeed very interesting, and we should have that document. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think we're going to be able to correct this -- this error. As I understand it, we didn't want to put in too many documents, but we will -- it is 1D 02366. That's my understanding. But we will be able to provide you with that -- with -- through a witness we'll be able to provide you with the exact part of that presidential transcript. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: May I continue? [Interpretation] I'm mentioning the Official Gazette but also the willingness to gather, for the sake of better organisation, members of all the nationalities that would, and I quote: "Will join those who are well organised, who wanted to introduce peace and order in a certain area." And of course I also mentioned a very clear political goal of the Croats, at least the way I understood it, and I quote: "It was clear to me from the moment I have joined the whole thing and from the moment I've been in this position, and this is the establishment and organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in keeping with the principles of European Community. In other words, the establishment of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the form of three national units. I believe that Croats will find this in their favour, but 14 the criterion should not be only the national composition of the population." My words are also about defence from the Serb aggression, and I said that we managed to by and large defend the Croatian territories in this area save for the Croatian Posavina. "Our standpoint is that we will not have any of the territory where we do not walk. I think that in this circle of people I can say this openly and I am not in favour of some kind of big-league politics which could deny what our forces have defended. We have not entered a single Serb village. We don't need a single Serb village." End of quote. At that time and today, I have respected Bosnia and Herzegovina and looked at it as a state of three peoples. The Serbian people are citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they constitute one-third of the total population, and in any solution their rights have to be protected. Why should we try and conquer the Serbian villages? Should we do that in order to expel the 2 population which is a normal result of war operations? No.I was against that. On that occasion, I handed over a letter to the representatives of the Croatian government and said to them, again I'm quoting myself: "We must talk about the number of issues that are exceptionally important for the functioning of the civilian authorities starting with the issue of customs which make it practically impossible for our companies to sell their goods to Croatia. We have to talk about border crossings, about commodity reserves, about the movement of goods, about border controls. We have to discuss all these issues that are central to the lives of people inhabiting this area." These are obviously issues that the coordination of the civilian authorities must resolve in coordination with the appropriate institutions of the Republic of Croatia. This is primarily about border- related issues, and I'm here referring to the border between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia, especially where those municipalities are concerned who were committed to coordinating a number of their duties and obligations at the level of Herceg-Bosna as a community. Your Honours, this was the first fully functioning state border of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the newly recognised state. If there is no cooperation, how can we define border crossings? How can we set up crews on both sides? How can we have border police? How can we have customs? After members of the same people had lived together in a single state for more than 110 years but were now divided by a new state border. So we were clearly establishing the border between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and making efforts to have it function as such. Please allow me to reflect on several very important areas mentioned also by the OTP, areas which they believed to be instruments of the joint criminal enterprise. Again, what we need is a context. This is something that I will not necessarily keep coming back to. Talking about finances, we can't discuss this without asking some questions, such as what was the currency that existed both in real and in purely formal terms? What was the currency that was actually being used? Were duties and taxes paid based on the customs earnings and to whom? What about the banks? Was it possible to make transfers from Bosnia and Herzegovina and send money abroad and vice versa for that matter? Were pensions being paid? What about the salaries of educational workers? What about police officers who were or were not receiving salaries and from whom? Who was providing salaries for those working in the judiciary, specifically judges and prosecutors? The financial laws that we had prepared immediately after we were appointed were adopted on the 28th of August, 1992, at an HVO HZ HB session. What is particularly noteworthy is that these were published in the Official Gazette number 3, and that was marked as having been issued in August 1992. If the Chamber cares to have a look, Official Gazette 1 and 2 date back to September 1992. It is quite obvious that the first to be published were these financial regulations, and those were then followed by -- by all the fundamental decisions on the establishment and functioning of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. This shows you in no uncertain terms what the priorities were of the HVO HZ HB as the provisional organ of executive government. As far as the possibilities for the functioning of -- of payment transactions without a currency to call our own, the use of the Croatian currency as a medium was the optimal technical solution, and I'm saying this as a professor. Bearing in mind the fact that most the foreign trade was with the Republic of Croatia, this would be a prime example of an optimum currency area. Most of the refugees were staying in Croatia at the time who were also using Croatia's currency. The regulations were changed, and this was mostly about criminal provisions, something being paid in Croatian dinars and German marks later on, and that's what it took for these regulations to start making sense. Formally speaking, at the time the official currency used in Bosnia and Herzegovina was the Yugoslav dinar, yet this same Yugoslavia had adopted a decision for this currency to be withdrawn from circulation. Believe me, monetary history had hardly seen a situation as absurd as this occur. The indictment talks about the import of goods from the Republic of Croatia bearing a special EU certificate with evidencing costs being covered. However, we must quote another reciprocal decision taken at the same session, which is also in evidence by the OTP, 5733. I quote: "The proposed decision on exporting goods to the Republic of Croatia for companies and other legal entities and natural persons in the HZ HB." This is obviously something that is reciprocal; the introduction of free trade, if you like. Those areas had never grown under that sort of burden before, and that is the sort of situation that prevails today. Not just between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, but, rather, throughout south-eastern Europe. This also applies to countries that are members of the EU. This opened a possibility for the economy to prosper in Bosnia and Herzegovina, leaving us in a position to export our goods to better advantage to our nearest neighbouring market, which was the Republic of Croatia, by using the certificate issued by the Chamber of Commerce. As the Chamber has already heard, at the beginning the duties and taxes were paid through non-resident accounts in Croatia itself. The opening of those accounts occurred pursuant to an inter-republican agreement on payments between Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. This agreement was reached in February 1992. The document number is 1D 01768. We've seen a number of such accounts that were being opened at the time, and some of these were held by bodies of Bosnia and Herzegovina's government and a number of players of Bosnia and Herzegovina's economy. This was the only way to do business, and it went on like that until the spring of 1993. We finally had the right conditions in Bosnia for proper transactions within the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that was when an order was issued to close those non-residential accounts for the most part in Croatia but to some extent, also, in neighbouring Slovenia. We have heard suggestions by the OTP that the decree on payments being made in Croatian dinars in the HZ HB was a de facto introduction of the Croatian currency as one that was to be used in the HZ HB. The Defence will show by adducing evidence that this is simply not true. Provisions 2 and 3 of that decree say that sub-accounts and not accounts in Croatian dinars may be opened with the Public Auditing Service, and I quote: “bearing a number 1 marked in the first codex from the left of ordinal number 1 in the RIR form. This is Prosecution Exhibit 447. All the accounts with the Public Auditing Service, the accounts of all the companies in the Apro Corporation, began with a 0, which meant that the initial accounts could only still be expressed in terms of the domestic currency, the Yugoslav dinar or, rather, the Bosnia,and Herzegovina dinar. Therefore over this entire period the Bosnia and Herzegovina dinar remained the official currency. As for the opening of these sub-accounts, this was only the very first step in order to have a payment system established in Bosnia and Herzegovina, without which no financial fiscal or legal system could have been envisaged. It was earlier on that most of the municipalities had already introduced the Croatian dinar as a parallel currency, or a currency used for non-cash payments. We shall be tendering a lot of documents in order to show this. As a provisional body of executive government, we accepted the first shipment of BH dinars as a legal currency. We tried using it. The Prosecutor mentioned the support that was sent to municipalities in Central Bosnia in new BH dinars. This was a decision that was taken in November 1992. Prosecution Exhibits 1063 and 1D 02127. Nonetheless, due to economic conditions, the BH dinar could never really get off the ground properly as a currency that would really be used and widely accepted as a medium for exchange, and this sort of situation prevailed throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. As I mentioned before, these non-residential accounts were being used until the conditions were in place for banks to start operating in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Prior to that time, there had been no banks at all. These new banks were now set up in keeping with the regulations defined by the National Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Appropriate amounts were paid that were required for registration. The amounts were paid in BH dinar. Licenses were issued, as is customary in all of the world's modern states. Document number is 1D 01765. Other measures were taken such as the introduction of the optical cable in order to get the telecommunications system up and running again. This made transactions possible now, and this was the single key element of the economic improvement that was to follow regardless of the consequences of war in HVO-controlled territory, where the economic situation was much better than in other areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The World Bank and the International Monetary Fund have carried out a number of studies showing this beyond doubt. And now something about the defence areas. There was a provision in the armed forces regulating each citizen's duty to contribute to the defence, and the way in which this is done is almost identical to that found in the Yugoslav law on All Peoples Defence. This provisional organ of executive government had no role in commanding the armed forces. This is shown by the provision on the armed forces, but also by the decision on the fundamental structure of the defence department defining clearly the structure of the department but also defining the responsibilities of all its components as well as the role of the Supreme Commander of the armed forces who was also the person who issued this decision. It must be noted that there is no mention anywhere of the HVO HZ HB in this decision, and the first decision bears the date of the 15th of September, 1992, which at that time was clearly already representing a civilian organ of the provisional executive government. Chapter 9 of this decision has already been addressed here, and this is about the responsibility of the HVO's Main Staff. A position was defined in relation to the defence department, mostly in terms of administrative issues, while the question of command and the use of forces was directly linked to the Supreme Commander, the president of the HZ HB. This paragraph, as is only to be expected, determines the chain of command that existed in the armed forces. One thing that must be noted, however, is that there is no mention there in any way of the HVO HZ HB as a provisional organ of executive government. This is Prosecution Exhibit P589. There will be Defence witnesses appearing to tell us what sort of information they were receiving at the time regarding the military situation on the ground and how that sort of information was reaching the HVO. Other Defence witnesses will be able to confirm that the HVO was not giving orders to the military component of the HVO, to the HVO's military units or its military police. The HVO HZ HB played no formal role in appointments in the armed forces. This was defined in the amendments to the decree on the armed forces in October 1992. We don't come across a single case of this being done before these changes if we look at all the documents available to us. I'm still talking about the same provision. It abolishes the possibility for the Supreme Commander to hand over certain duties in terms of command and control of the armed forces to a provisional organ of executive government. It is quite clear that through these changes the HVO HZ HB loses any jurisdiction that it may have had prior to my appointment as president of the provisional body of executive government on the 14th of August. These changes were perfectly in keeping with the HVO being defined as a provisional organ of executive government regarding civilian issues. The decision, from the same decree, on the methodology to be applied when drafting defence plans was retained from the previous legislation related to the general notion of All Peoples Defence and social self-protection. Each socio-political community from the federation to the municipality, each legal subject, a company, for example, a bank -- a bank, a local commune, a school, all of those needed a defence plan, and these defence plans, of 15 course, had a civilian character, and no use of the armed forces was implied. That sort of inertia went on in the BH republican legislation. I'm referring to Articles 109 through 112 of the Law On Defence. When looking at the framework of measures that were being taken in the HZ HB in terms of security and fighting crime, the important ones are those that have to do with internal affairs and with the judiciary and general administration. When it comes to the judiciary, and this is confirmed by their reports, the goal was to activate the work of the courts and also to establish the system of military judiciary, and that's why the initial provisions were drafted. In the former system, the overall judicial system was completely separated from the military judiciary, which was within the system of the Yugoslav People's Army. During the general transition process towards a democratic system, and one should bear in mind that the JNA had officially been proclaimed an aggressor, interventions were necessary in order to draw closer to at least the minimal democratic standards. The second objective problem which necessitated changes and interventions in the judiciary system was this: There was no single judiciary proceedings that could be completed and become valid if there was no third instance with the right of hearing appeals. Bearing in mind that Sarajevo was cut off, the departments of the Supreme Court were established as well as the departments of the republican Public Prosecutor, which was a common practice that was later on applied in the districts by the Sarajevo authorities. The Defence will show that a political consensus for this system was achieved between the HDZ and the SDA and that the staff in the judiciary could be appointed in that way. Besides setting up judicial bodies and creating the minimum legal basis for their functioning, we also tried to introduce particular operative programmes in order to fight crime, and this implies what is important within the context of this Tribunal are war crimes amongst other things. The documents of the Prosecution speak that on the 22nd of March, 1993, the vice-president Zubak reported about the application of the programme in practice. He also stated that numerous successes had been achieved in the campaign, and he also added that there is a lot more room for improvement, and this improvement could be achieved if we engaged some well-equipped experts. This is Prosecution Exhibit P 1703. At a special session on the 11th of August, 1993, 21 conclusions were passed which, according to the minutes, represented, quote: “a legal and organisational framework for the HZ HB to be established on the fundaments of legality.” This is document P 4111. A special coordination body was established, and I was one of its members. This body tried to launch a number of activities that are illustrated by the documents. The conclusions which were passed reveal the intention of the HVO HZ HB to deal with crime and to curb it, but it -- it also arises from these conclusions that the objective force lies in the Presidency of the HZ HB and in the municipalities. That's why as the necessary prerequisite, if we wanted to achieve any success, was to ask for the political support of the Presidency of the HZ HB and the Executive Board of the HDZ. Without their support, we could not embark on such a demanding programme. Because of the information that we received internally from the international community, we included on our agenda at the session of the 18th of August the following: In order to protect property and lives of Muslims in Ljubuski, measures and activities should be taken to curb irresponsible behaviour of the individuals and groups. This is Exhibit number 4276. There's another interesting remark, and I quote: "Within the area of jurisdiction, we should build the policy in order to institute stricter punishments for the perpetrators of aggravated crimes: violent crimes, robbery and armed robbery." The implementation of the tasks which were defined by members of the provisional organ of executive government may be followed through the reports of various prosecutors' offices and the courts in the Department Of Judiciary and House Of Representatives, which was established ten days later. Allowing to the position of its representatives, it took over the leading position in this type of programme. I'm referring to documents 1D 02371, 1D 02368. For example, the government drafted a report on the situation of crime and evaluated the situation and measures that were taken and presented that report to the House of Representatives of the HR HB in December 1993. Document number is 1D 01977. Before that, on the 18th of September, 1993, I sent a letter to the Supreme Commander and the president of the House Of Representatives containing proposals as to what should be done in order to overcome the state of chaos that we were facing at that time. People who were members of that coordination board were all unique in adopting the same position. Document number is 1D 01813. We established a commission to establish war crimes whose task was to investigate any type of potential war crimes committed in the territory of Herceg-Bosna regardless of the perpetrator and regardless of the victim. This commission cooperated with the local prosecutor's office as has been envisaged by the document on its foundation. Such an early reference to the Tribunal, even before the Tribunal was actually established, speaks of the willingness of the HVO HZ HB to support its establishment and willingness to help it to process all forms of war crimes, which is also corroborated by a letter to the first Prosecutor of this Tribunal, Mr. Goldstone. The document number is 1D 02007. Regardless of the establishment of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the government of the HR HB launched a sweeping operation, Operation Spider, in June 1994, which involved all the competent ministries as well as some of the task forces from the Republic of Croatia in order to apprehend and process all the perpetrators of all the crimes that had been recorded up to then. The members of this Trial Chamber has already seen that the competent bodies recorded all the crimes during the war, and based on those records this wide-reaching action had been launched. In a document that I signed on behalf of the government, it says as follows and I quote: "The purpose of this action is to -- for the action to last over a long period of time with a tight time schedule and to combine operative prevention, repressive, and crime prevention measures and apprehend all those people for which there is a reasonable suspicion that they had committed crimes." These people had to be processed, investigated, and taken to justice. The document number is 1D 01249. The witnesses in this courtroom has already spoken about the results of this action, and there will be more to talk about the results of this action. The responsibility for processing the crimes committed during the war was taken over by the judiciary of the federation and later on Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent part of the tripartite division of power in whose establishment I participated as a member of government [Indiscernible]. I also want to mention that the Parliament of the Federation adopted the Law on Amnesty which does not exculpate those who committed war crimes but what needs to be said at this moment is this: On the 18th of February, 1996, the so-called Rome Agreement was signed and I witnessed that. I was in Rome at the time. This agreement establishes the rules of the road which defined how can local courts in Bosnia and Herzegovina process war crimes. According to the rules of the road, as the agreement would become to be known,local courts can try war crimes only with a prior consent of the International War Crimes Tribunal in The Hague. If this is maybe the time for our next break, I am just embarking on a new chapter in my presentation.
