utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The hearing is resumed. Mr. Prlic, you have the floor. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: Thank you, Mr. President. Just to make one mistake in transcript that was asked by lawyer of Mr. Pusic. On page 37, line 25, it should be written Puljic, not Pusic. I mentioned the name Puljic. [Interpretation] During the break I tried to reduce to a certain extent my presentation, but I don't think I will be able to finish today. A few words about refugees. I believe that the Prosecutor’s claim, at least quoting the indictment, that this activity is a war crime represents an impermissible simplification of the dramatic humanitarian problem of the status and care of refugees and displaced persons. The decision on the status of refugees which was passed by the HZ HB only towards the end of 1992, after all the municipalities had already regulated this area, was an attempt to lay down the groundwork needed to introduce a system into this issue. It transpires quite clearly from the text of the decision that it was oriented toward citizens and that it is not by any means discriminatory, all the more so as it referred to a very loosely defined territory of the HZ HB. The organ that I was a member of forbade during the war any transfer of real estate in order to prevent any transactions under duress. The office for refugees was a very small organisation. It had only 12 members of staff and did not have funds for work, and as we heard, there were over a hundred thousand refugees in our small territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. Normally I would not interrupt but my colleague insists on me interrupting because of the gravity of the error that is being -- that is on the text over here. It was "not a well-defined" as opposed to "well-defined." There is a big difference to that. We would appreciate if perhaps Mr. Prlic would slow down, articulate, so that the translators would then properly translate this, but this is an error that I must correct. It's on page 65, line 7. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. [Interpretation] We're talking about a very small body. Towards the end of June 1993, the interim executive body established a staff that would organise and coordinate work on looking after the displayed persons and refugees. As it transpires from the documents, this was established due to the gravity of the humanitarian crisis in order to, I quote, "guide and coordinate the work of the various bodies that were dealing with refugees." At the peak of the humanitarian crisis in July 1993, the HVO HZ HB passed the following conclusions: Take all the possible measures in order to protect the civilian population within the zones of war operations in which new refugees and displaced persons arriving into the territory of the HZ HB should be taken into account -- should be taken into account. The headquarters for the organisation and coordination of the work of the bodies looking after refugees and displaced persons are duty-bound to arrange the unimpeded departure of civilians, in accordance with their wishes, to third countries. The work --working group of the office for refugees and displaced persons should continue contacts with the government of the Republic of Croatia with a view to the efficiently dealing with the problem of accommodation and transit of refugees from the territory of HZ HB, establish contacts with the UNHCR with the view to opening the transit centre for the refugees in the territory of HZ HB. That would be under the auspices of this international organisation. And finally, inform the ministry of the foreign affairs of the Republic of Croatia with the issue. The document is number P 3560. All these conclusions are -- apply across the board to the citizens, to the civilians and there is no reference to any particular ethnic group that would be allowed to leave the area of war operations. And it is only within this context that all the other conclusions had to be reviewed. In order to provide for the protection of civilians, it is only logical to establish contacts with the UNHCR and the office for refugees of the only country to which the refugees could go to, and that was the Republic of Croatia. Members of the Trial Chamber, at that time of the 19 members of my family in Mostar, only the two of us remained living in Mostar. Some of the witnesses from the international community mentioned the issue of the transit centre which was indeed opened with their assistance. The report on the work of the office for refugees and displaced persons from early 1994 indicates that in October 1993 a transit centre had been opened. It was mentioned by several witnesses from international organisations. Thanks to their support it was opened in biggest hotel in Ljubuski, and it is stressed in this Prosecution exhibit, 6324, several thousand people were housed there before they left for third countries. For the most part those were Croats and not, as one could conclude from some of the testimonies before this Court, that the initiative to set up the transit centre was in fact to serve the purpose of ethnically cleansing the Muslims. When we're talking about the passage of humanitarian convoys it is important to mention in this context the agreement on the free passage of convoys, but also some other humanitarian issues. That was signed on our initiative by the HVO HZ HB and the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Makarska, in the Republic of Croatia, on the 8th of July, 1993. This agreement envisages for the cooperation and organisation of humanitarian aid convoys, and there were some teething troubles related to the adopting of certain protocols. It functioned more or less well as is indicated in the reports originating from the office. The purpose of the protocol was to avoid any arbitrary decisions and to impose quite specific rules, and it is quite clearly defined by international law what humanitarian aid is. Cigarettes cannot be considered as humanitarian aid if they are subject to taxation, for instance. This agreement envisaged, as the operative body, a joint commission that included representatives of the international community, and they themselves stressed that the protocol at the time solved all the problems, the way in which the items on the humanitarian convoys were to be checked was also defined, as were all the elements needed to ensure that humanitarian aid is distributed. Prosecution Exhibit P 3346. There were no examples of convoy with international aid setting off and then being stopped or of convoys not being approved by the Herceg-Bosna bodies. Now as regards the transparency of the work and the so-called Croatisation I will leave aside. I will let the witnesses say something about that. Let me now say something about the relationship between the HVO HZ HB and the Presidency of the HZ HB. The relationship between those two bodies is quite clearly defined by their respective Rules of Procedure. We in the executive body as professionals wanted to have transparent relations. The minutes mention what one of our future witnesses will say -- will say, Zoran Buntic, the head of the judiciary and general administration department where he says, and I quote: "The proposal is made for the Presidency to meet more often and that the respective competencies of the HVO and the Presidency be clearly defined by the Presidency." That's P 00534. The 7th session in October 1992, I quote: "It is necessary to provide political support from the Presidency of the HZ HB in order to establish a unified system of customs and tax on the whole territory of the HZ HB. That's P 00578. The character of the relationship defines the needs to report to the departments and to the provisional bodies or, rather, that those departments and those provisional bodies should report to those who appointed them, the presidents of the municipalities who were members of the Presidency of the HZ HB. If you look -- if you cast a cursory look at all the reports, it is obvious that this is a compilation of reports on the work of the departments and commissions, and on the first few pages the work at the sessions of the HVO HZ HB is described. We're talking about Prosecution Exhibits P 128, P 04611, P 04735. It is obvious that this is a report filed by the HVO as a collective organ and the departments that is meant for the Presidency of the HZ HB, because there is no need for the departments and members of the HZ HB to report to each other, and this is stressed at the session of the HVO HZ HB. Let me quote: "After all the reports on the -- on the work of the HVO HZ HB for the period between the 1st of January, 1993, until the 30th of June,1993, are completed, they will be submitted to the Presidency of the HZ HB." This is Exhibit P 04220. The Defence witnesses will provide explanations to the Trial Chamber about the conclusions of the HVO HZ HB that were sent to the Presidency of the HZ HB on the 13th of July, 1993. That's document P 03413, where due to the situation that HVO HZ HB was informed about, another proposal is made to Mr. Mate Boban to call an urgent meeting of the Presidency of the HZ HB, the Presidency of the HDZ, and the presidents of the Municipal Boards of the HDZ in order to organise the defence. Those conclusions were passed a month before that, on the 15th of June, 1993. That's document 1D 01668. After the -- the provisional organ was notified about the attacks by the BH army on Travnik, Kiseljak, Vitez, Kakanj, and the persecution that Croats in Zenica, Sarajevo, and other places where they were in a minority faced. Apparently the institutions that had the authority and that could do something in this area failed to do what was in their power. The situation deteriorated. In particular after a BH army attack in the wider Mostar area on the 30th of June, 1993, and the attack on Fojnica with the fighting continuing in the Central Bosnia area. And we were prompted to resubmit the conclusions of the 15th of June once again, hoping that the institutions, the competent institutions, would do what we were not empowered to decide. The presidential transcript dated the 10th of November, 1993, where the composition of the future government of the HR HB is discussed, I speak about my visit to Banja Luka, and I quote: "I was with Komarica on Saturday evening. It is consolidated. It is a little bit better for the Croats. They're not being mobilised anymore, but -- and some other agencies - illegible - they have to do work obligation but this cannot be prevented. They're picking apples, and that is better than if they have to go to serve in the army." That's Prosecution Exhibit P 06581. The purpose of my visit to Banja Luka, and I was invited by Bishop Komarica, was to make it possible for Croats not to be called up to serve in the Serbian army, which at that time was the basic reason they quoted when they wanted to leave this area. So the purpose of my visit was to ensure that Croats will continue to reside in those parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina which could never become part of the HR HB, which is contrary to the Prosecution allegation about the interest that Croats might have in moving into areas that are defined as areas with Croatian majority. It is ironic that in one of the courtrooms of this Tribunal a judgement was delivered about the events that led to the mass exodus of Croats, more than 100.000 of them. The military commander of this area was sentenced to three and a half years in prison for these events, leading to these consequences; yet in another courtroom this mass exodus is actually reverse ethnic cleansing that Croats are responsible for. For areas that in the very same indictment are not only described or defined as the goal of the Croatian political leadership but areas from which non-Croats were supposed to be expelled. Where is the logic in that? Even a cursory glance at the Official Gazettes show that they contained a large number of appointments that I signed. The character of these decisions -- of these decisions, the decision-making at the sessions, this is something that I explained to a certain extent, but I would like to say now that the body that I chaired and in whose work I participated wanted to achieve full equality in ethnic terms with the Muslim people. The fact that this agreement existed can be seen from a letter from the SDA to the Electronic Power Company of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which still exists - where protocol that was signed is mentioned and appointments -- and appointments are mentioned, and let me quote: "The appointed representatives of the SDA are authorised to take and to perform tasks and to coordinate work on constituting and organising the affairs within the framework of the provisional organisation of the HZ Herceg-Bosna." That's 1D 1560. Yet another example, the payroll for May 1993 for hydroelectric plant in Rama. The largest employer in Prozor municipality, the municipality to which the crime base in this case is linked, indicates that judging by the names among the 49 employees at least 20 are Muslim. That's 1D 01991, or a quote from the report on the work of the department for judiciary and public administration for 1992. After getting the approval by the municipal HVO for the proposed candidates of Croatian - from the Croatian ethnic community and the approval of the Regional Board of the SDA for the proposed candidates of the Muslim - from the Muslim ethnic background and in light of the conclusions from the session of the Presidency of the 17th of October, 1992, the proposal for the decision on the appointment was drafted, and then the names follow. It is clear that the SDA agreed with the proposals. Defence documents will show that, for instance, of the eight judges elected to the Supreme Court Department in Mostar, three are Muslims. That's 1D 2124. Again, 8 of the 13 judges in the Lower Court in Mostar were Muslims, as were more than 50 per cent of the employees as shown by document 1D 02381. The Official Gazettes indicate that the director of the Vodoprivreda company was Dzemal Cosic. The deputy director of the public auditing service is Jusuf Skaljic, as shown as P 00672. Or let us go back to the sessions. P 824. Members of the commission for regulations Aid Glavovic, as the chairman, Damjan Vlasic, Ante Bijuk, Mahmut Jugo. They are members of the commission. While members of the management board of the post and telecommunications public company are Ilija Kozul, Enes Santic from Mostar, Verenko Cubela from Livno, Branko Colak from Siroki Brijeg, and Enes Sehic from Novi Travnik. So two out of five are Muslims. In December 1992, that's from the minutes of the session, you can see my words, I asked the heads of all the departments and sub-departments to draft proposals for the appointments of persons of Muslim ethnic background for one of the following sessions of the HVO HZ HB. That's document P 921. In mid-January 1993, again at the session, it is said, I quote: "The bodies and services of the HVO HZ HB should submit, in the course of the day, the situation as regards the participation of Muslims and Muslims in the managerial positions in the bodies, organs, and administrative organisations of the HZ HB." That's document 1D 818. Now allow me to say a few words about our relations with the government in Sarajevo. I can say that our relations were quite correct. Most of the members of the government actually was in the free territory so that we were able to meet quite often. Jure Pelivan, the president, Zarko Primorac who will testify as the Finance Minister. Muhamed Logo, his deputy, Tomislav Krsticevic, transport minister. Alija Delimustafic, minister of the interior, and other members of the cabinet, Jahic, Muratovic, Raguz, to name but a few, would come to visit us and we talked about arranging some joint activities. We took part in programmes on TV and on radio. As for Avdo Campara, the secretary of the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I made arrangements with him to organise the session - a session of the Assembly in Mostar. The provisional organ at the very beginning of its operation took the following stand: All the documents passed by the HVO HZ HB should co-exist with the regulations of the republic or the regulations of the republic should be complied with wherever possible, which clearly shows the view this organ took towards the institutions of the republic. That's Prosecution Exhibit P 00543. The provisions were very clear about the level of responsibility about everything, and that also applies to cooperation with the institutions at the level of the Republic. Article 7 of the Decree on the structure and remit of the departments and commissions says these bodies should work with the republican bodies in preparing the laws defining the policies of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and also to prepare other laws and regulations of a more general nature whenever these are in relation to the equal status enjoyed by all the constituent ethnic groups in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the start of my activity, just after my appointment, I sent a letter to the government in Sarajevo, based on the conclusions of the HVO HZ HB, explaining the need to act but also our willingness for the situation to return to normal. I quote: "Please find attached the regulations passed by the provisional organ of executive government of the HVO, the objective being to normalise living conditions and to get the legal system in the liberated areas fully operational again." If you look at these, it will become perfectly clear that we tried to remain perfectly in keeping and consistent with the republican provisions and regulations. The circumstances surrounding this were difficult. There was a war on. There was a lot of destruction, disruptions to traffic and telecommunications, lack of assistance or support by the republican organs. It was necessary to take action and to define certain rules and pass certain legal instruments with a view to overcoming this state of chaos and overall anarchy that had come about as a result of the war. The document number is 1D 01558. So we submitted to the republican government all the first legal instruments that we passed as provisional organs of executive government. In the autumn of 1992, I was authorised by the government to act on behalf of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this is document 1D 2147, when it came to cooperation with international organisations especially as concerned shipments of humanitarian aid. I was also authorised to coordinate any measures between the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the one hand and the HVO HZ HB on the other -- or, rather, and I'm quoting the decision itself: "To be involved in making appropriate financial arrangements regarding any defence activities." It is against this background that one must interpret measures that were taken in relation to the office for military production, for example. Bearing in mind my powers, I tried to make sure that the regulations passed by the HZ HB were fully consistent, provisional as they were and temporary. I also permanently took into account the fact that they should be - that they should remain within the framework of the legal system of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. For the most part these were implementing regulations that we adopted, and we tried not to ever go into any issues that would require, so to speak, a higher level of democratic legitimacy such as, for example, property, relations, organizing elections, and such like. Needless to say, I worked within the powers that I had. I tried to help. I tried to help get civilian life organised, and I had tried to ease the difficulties faced by all of our citizens. Despite my other duties and commitments, I travelled abroad. I worked with the office for refugees of the Republic of Croatia in a bid to secure humanitarian aid from this country that happened to be the single most important donor of humanitarian aid to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I think witnesses will address this issue. Another thing that shows the scope of work of the provisional executive organ of executive government and the willingness to enter into productive relations with the government in Sarajevo is the letter, already admitted into evidence, that led to the much-debated meeting of the 18th of April, 1993, and this was a meeting referred to by a number of witnesses. The date on this letter is the 2nd of April, 1993. 1D 0194. It was a letter to the head of the ECMM which had offered coordination for the talks. In this letter I proposed the following subjects for discussion, which was within my powers: “The production and distribution of electricity; maintenance of roads through liberated areas; prevention of all forms of illegal activity: smuggling, including smuggling of humanitarian aid; reconstruction of schools and taking care of other forms of education; taking care of retired persons; and putting up refugees and their return.” End of quotation. The start of the clashes in mid-April, as we heard confirmed by a number of witnesses, changed the agenda of the 18th of April, 1993, meeting organised by ECMM. The meeting was attended by a member of the Presidency of the republic, Franjo Boras, as well as Ejup Ganic and General Petkovic. As prime minister of the transitional government of the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I was pushing for specific steps to be taken as quickly as possible. In a bid to achieve that, I wrote a letter to the RBH government in May 1993. I quote: "As the deadlines are very short for these activities, I think it would be useful if you could immediately prepare appropriate documents for the hand-over itself." The document number is 1D 1598. This continuity of various activities is also demonstrated by the minutes of the first meeting of the government of Herceg-Bosna and the Sarajevo government. This meeting was held in my office in Mostar on the 6th of April, 1994. No representatives of the international community were present, yet we managed to agree a number of practical steps much like those that I had been proposing in April the previous year. Representatives of both sides agreed on the way the customs bodies should function, the return of refugees, reconstruction of the electricity system and the electrical energy system, and a number of infrastructural interventions in Mostar itself. The document number is 1D 1953. We met on a number of other occasions, as well, including a visit to Sarajevo in March and in April 1994. Needless to say, we dealt with those issues jointly at a later stage, bearing in mind the fact that I had become deputy prime-minister of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or rather, deputy prime minister of the Federation as of June 1994. Most of the ministers from Herceg-Bosna's government became members of the Republican or Federation government. This is where I'd like to move on to another issue, and this is something that has been discussed a great deal in this courtroom. This is an issue that features very prominently in the indictment itself, the so-called 15 January ultimatum. The 15th of January, 1993, of course. The Chamber knows exactly which document I'm talking about. That is why I wish to point one thing out at the very outset. This decision, the way I understood it then, 15 years ago, and I can confirm this now, was no ultimatum. It was never discussed or considered as any form of ultimatum, and that certainly wasn't how it was written, neither was it meant to be taken as an ultimatum. If we put the decision into perspective, if you know what sort of information was available to us at the time, or what we were led to believe, it is easy to understand that the objective of this decision was to set up a Joint Command of the HVO and the BH army. As far as I remember, all of us back in early 1993 believed, especially taking into account the developments that followed the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia, as well as the kind of information that we were receiving at the time, that the war was over. This might strike one as naive from our present standpoint. Nonetheless, I do remember that at the -- a meeting of this provisional executive body of government, many of us were saying that the war was now over, or at least that it would soon be over, and we started thinking about how to get our companies up and running again, how to create jobs for soldiers who would in the meantime have been demobilised. A decision was drafted and adopted pursuant to a request of the head of the Croatian delegation of those international talks, Mr. Boban, the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, who was also the head of the negotiating team for the Croats. No one at the time had any reason to doubt the accuracy of Mr. Boban's information on such agreement as has been reached. Likewise, there was no reason to go and review Mr. Boban's instructions to the effect that we should take a decision to reflect both the letter and the spirit of that agreement. Why doubt his honesty? Why challenge his instructions? After all, he was perfectly authorised to issue such instructions. They wanted us to draft and issue a decision that for all practical intents will have been tantamount to implementation of the peace proposal. Of course, the decision called for avoidance of any conflict between the HVO and the BH army in free territory. Your Honours, we must bear in mind the fact that the BH army and the HVO were components of a joint armed force. This is specifically shown in the order on lifting the blockade of Sarajevo city issued by the president of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, on the 16th of October, 1992. Item 1 of this order reads, and I quote: "The armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina (the BH army and the HVO) will immediately start preparing actions to lift the blockade of Sarajevo city by military means." 1D 02432. Unfortunately, tensions soon escalated between the two armed forces in the same territory despite best efforts on both parts and the good faith shown on both sides to find an appropriate solution. This was the reason that as we have witnessed during the Prosecution case throughout the war and well before the clashes between those units broke out there had been permanent and ongoing efforts to find a pattern based on which to organise a Joint Command of the HVO and the BH army, a pattern that would have been deemed acceptable by both parties. There was some degree of success in this respect in the autumn of 1992 on the eve of the fall of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic, let me interrupt you. You quoted this document which seems very important to me, 1D 2032. It is an order signed by Izetbegovic about the siege of Sarajevo. I have the document in front of me. It was not translated. I therefore do not have the English translation. In the binder we have the B/C/S version but no English translation, whilst this document may be extremely important. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: Mr. President, I think that the number 2432, but I'm not so sure that -- I said 2432.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In any event, Your Honour, all of these documents will be made available through witnesses in the appropriate languages in due time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's wait and see. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] At that press conference members of the new command took part, Officer Jasmin Jaganac, General Ante Prkacin, the commander of the 1st Mostar Brigade Arif Pasalic, as well as the commander of the District Staff commander here of Zenica Dzemal Merdan, 1D 1424. The information about partial implementation of Vance-Owen Plan arrived on the 15th of January in the afternoon. That morning we held a regular session. On that day, we were informed that a meeting had been held in Zagreb between Mate Boban; Alija Izetbegovic, the president of the Republic of Croatia; Franjo Tudjman; and the co-chairpersons of the conference for the former Yugoslavia, so it was only logical to find a link between these events. Document number is P 1146. The fact that it was believed about this decision that it was based on the information that the agreement had been reached may be seen in the preamble, and I quote: "In keeping with the agreements reached so far and signed at the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia (in the Geneva agreements)." Document number P 1146. Although it is very difficult to be absolutely certain about everything, when writing this decision we had in our mind the whole context of international agreements starting with Cutileiro's plan about establishing three constituent units in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the conclusion of the London conference, the joint proposal of the SDA and the HDZ about the organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which later on gave the foundation for the Vance-Owen Plan, up to the first comprehensive peace proposal - the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Let us not forget that the draft of the constitutional organisation for Bosnia and Herzegovina which was drafted by the working group of the Geneva conference for the former Yugoslavia was adopted by the Security Council of the United Nations on the 16th of November, 1992. The document number is P 752. Would it be too much to believe at the time that the international community had finally helped us to draft a peace agreement with a constitutional package ready to be implemented? I don't think so. Especially bearing in mind the vast quantity of time and energy that was spent by everybody who participated in these negotiations. The purpose of the decision which says in article 4 clearly, and I quote: "The temporary and valid up to the moment when the Geneva agreements on the organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina is signed," and this should never have been implemented by force. As far as what I was thinking at the time, I would like to draw your attention to my words that were recorded by ECMM, and I quote my own words: "Mr. Prlic said that the HVO would not do anything in order to implement the decision sent to units in BH with the deadline on the 20th of January by force. Copy enclosed." Document number P 1215. As one can easily see, the decision was delivered to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to the department of defence. This was an issue that had been resolved apparently, and this was an integral solution aimed at achieving peace. One has to bear in mind that Vance-Owen Peace Agreement envisaged a lot of Croats in the provinces where the Croats did not constitute a majority before and where about 20.000 soldiers of the HVO fought in the war. During the same transition period, these same soldiers should have been under the command of the BH army, and they accepted that. As far as the nature of the decision is concerned as reported by ECMM at a joint meeting organised in order to resolve any possible misunderstandings, and I quote: "With regard to the decision of the HVO itself to take over the direct control over all the troops that still remain in its territory up to the 20th of January, him," meaning Prlic, "regrets deeply that the agreement on creating the joint command between BiH army and the HVO failed after five or six months of negotiations. Still this decision --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Can the counsel of Dr. Prlic check the figures in English because in the interpretation I get in French where we have direct interpretation from B/C/S into French, I often don't have the same figures. For instance, line 25, page 92 [As interpreted], I heard 1.212. I see 1215 in English. Page 83, line 14, I have 28th of January and I heard 20th of January in French. Please check because we might find it very difficult to locate the documents later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First and foremost, this is a written text which is has been provided to the translation booths in Croatian of course. That's number one. Number two, there are several in the 10s, perhaps even in the 20s of errors that have occurred. We haven't stopped to correct each and every one of them. We will be going over the text, and we will insist on a correction on every one of these, and that goes for the numbers as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Prlic. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] According to his words, and I'm still being quoted, "The commander of BiH agreed with this decision, and this is nothing but a direct consequence of the document that was signed by Boban in Geneva. In reality, he emphasised that this decision would not lead to any major changes because, for example, in Mostar the 1st Brigade of BiH is already under the command of the HVO." The same document, P 1215 is the number of the document. Documents in this case has -- have already shown, and the witnesses of the Defence will confirm that the conflict in Gornji Vakuf started much earlier than the 15th of January, much before that. The time does not allow me to provide all the details of the events that ensued. However, it goes without saying that the whole situation was overcome in an exceptionally conciliatory spirit, and again I would like to draw your attention to the same document of the ECMM dated 19th January, and I quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it should read that it -- one should say, line 19. In other words, it's axiomatic. It's absolutely certain that this situation was resolved in overcoming this situation, that is in the spirit of peace and cooperation, and I would urge, I would urge, I would urge Dr. Prlic to please slow down, enunciate, pause. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] I quote: "After a minor misunderstanding and an exchange of letters, letters enclosed and copies between the government of Herceg-Bosna, Prlic, and the Presidency of BiH, Prlic requested for a meeting to be organised as soon as possible between Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban in Split. Such a meeting is necessary because many issues have to be clarified and resolved particularly in this time of uncertainty which was created by the new developments in Geneva." I would like to say at this moment one more thing that is very interesting in this context. I have read a publication, the International Conference For The Former Yugoslavia, the official documents which has about 1.630 pages altogether and which contains the reports of the co-chairpersons, the Secretary-General of the United Nations, and I have also read the so-called COREA reports by the representatives of the European Community in these negotiations, which were submitted with his book and later withdrawn. There was no single place in which I could find a reference to the so-called ultimatum in January 1993. What I did find, however, amongst other things, with regard to the negotiations which took place in that month, was this that I'm going to quote in English from page 727: [In English] "In that time the Croats signed all elements of the peace package proposed by the co-chairmen and that international community," again quoting, "continuously support the peace package and invite other two sides to sign the whole peace package so that its implementation might start as soon as possible in order to finish the war." [Interpretation] At the end, I would conclude this issue -- this issue by saying that the decision on the withdrawal of the decision dated 15 January 1993 was passed when it was proven that there was no common willingness of the Croatian and Muslim leaderships to implement it. For example, the president of the HZ HB, Boban, in keeping with his competencies ordered that the decision be suspended in the same manner he had decided for the decision to be passed. We saw the letter written in his own hand on the paper of the hotel intercontinental in Zagreb. Mate Boban wrote, and I quote: "I order you that in the course of the day you schedule an emergency meeting of the HVO HZ HB and change or amend item number 5," document number 1D 0820.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the Court's indulgence, if Mr. Prlic could read that last paragraph again slowly. For instance, there is no word, "for example." There isn't -- that wasn't uttered. It's not in the text. I know because my colleague instructs me that it isn't, and I am familiar with the text as well. Because the point is that Dr. Prlic is trying to make here is just as Mr. Boban had ordered the decision to be drafted and issued, Mr. Boban again, given his responsibilities and authorities, orders to have it withdrawn or put on ice, as it were. So if Dr. Prlic could read that again, because those are his words, not my words, and what I say is not evidence, but what he says can be used as evidence, whatever weight the Trial Chamber wishes to give.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may add an observation. I'm not quite sure whether Mr. Prlic actually wanted to speak of a Croatian Muslim leadership on line 6 of page 86. That's rather surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I think the intention was that the leaderships of the Croats and the Muslims could not find the common ground, the willingness to go forward as we saw because it makes sense we see that the Croats as one -- one said, they always had a pen in their pocket ready to sign all these agreements, and in fact we see continuously the Croats signing agreement after agreement after agreement after agreement where Izetbegovic says one thing in the morning and another thing in the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In short, Mr. Karnavas, there's a hyphen missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Probably. Probably, but I think the point is, the point that we're trying to drive at is that the Croats are constantly signing, the others are being cajoled to go ahead, and Dr. Prlic is saying there seems to be a lack of willingness, which is a generous way of putting the Muslims don't want to go forward, but nonetheless, you know, the person who issued the decision, which is Boban, you know, is the one that now is also ordering them to withdraw it, hence who has the power, who has the responsibility. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the best thing to do is for you to read that sentence you quoted again, but do it slowly, and also for the transcript, I see my name line 11. For once I didn't say anything. So it's Judge Trechsel, not me. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: I don't know really what is the problem. Mr. Karnavas speaks so fast that everything is possible to be translated. I delivered 1.000 speeches, and I haven't spoke so slowly in my life, and there is problem in that. So I am going to repeat once again. [Interpretation] "At the end I would like to conclude about this issue that decision to withdraw the decision issued on the 15th of January was issued because it had been shown that there was no willingness on the part of the Croatian and Muslim leaderships to implement it." So the president of the HZ HB, Mr. Boban, in keeping with his competencies, ordered for the decision to be suspended in the same way he had ordered the decision to be issued. We saw a letter written in his own hand on the letterheaded paper of the Intercontinental Hotel in Zagreb. Mate Boban, the president of the HZ HB, wrote, I quote: "I order you to schedule an emergency meeting of the HVO HZ HB in the course of the day and change or amend item number 5." Document number 1D 0820. And as we have already seen, the executive power did exactly what Mr. Boban had ordered it to do and what Mr. Izetbegovic wanted. Immediately after that, both of them - document number P 1329 signed the statement on the immediate stop of conflict. It is well known, and this Trial Chamber is aware of the fact that in March the Muslim side signed the integral package of Vance-Owen Plan. In that month we, however, received a request from the government in Sarajevo to organise or establish districts in the territories of Mostar and Livno that bore no resemblance to the areas about which an agreement had already existed at least between the Muslim and the Croat sides within the framework of Vance-Owen Plan. Subsequently the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina also passed a decision on the implementation of that plan. And regardless of the fact that a bilateral implementation of the plan had been agreed on, attempts were being made on the ground to implement the decisions on the establishment of districts, which can really be considered a two-faced policy. At the same time, the HVO HZ HB at its session held on the 3rd of April, 1993, adopted a programme of measures intended to implement Vance-Owen Plan, which was a very complex task, a very tall order. Later on, the federation of Bosniak and Croats was implemented with the help of the international community over a period of almost five years. These conclusions very clearly say that the HVO HZ HB and the President Mate Boban was present at the session, was ready to dissolve Herceg-Bosna. And as for the interim bodies of the executive bodies, they were willing to transform into the provinces as envisaged by that peace agreement. So those who tried to implement districts and at the same time signed agreements on the implementation of Vance-Owen Plan were engaged in two-faced policies. The Prosecution is trying to establish a link between the session of the provisional organ of the executive government of the 3rd of April with the outbreak of the conflict, and there is no basis for this link. Whoever accepts a peace plan, whoever is ready to disband the provisional institutions that had been established, the party whose forces are several times smaller than those of the other side would not start the kind of conflict that happened in that month. Defence witnesses will show that there is no causal link between the 3rd of April meeting and the beginning of the conflict in April. To a certain extent, the joint communique about the Croat-Muslim relations speaks to that. On the 24th of April, this communique was presented after talks in Zagreb by Izetbegovic and Mate Boban where they say that all the misunderstandings in the relations between the Croat and Muslim peoples should be resolved using political means, that there is no reason for any conflicts. All units are given orders to cease hostilities, to release the prisoners, and to determine the responsibility and the intentions of the formations and units for the outbreak of the hostilities. That's P 2088. I cannot now cover the whole time line in this overview, but in my opinion, as our session draws to a close, I would like to say that perhaps the last effort to prevent the conflict was the implementation of the conclusions from the Medjugorje meeting on the 18th of May where specific deadlines were set for the bilateral implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan, which contrary to the Prosecution's allegations was not dead by early May. As the prime minister elect of the Republican government with the support of both parties, I really tried to do everything I could to set up the joint government and the Joint Command. In the short period while we were waiting for the provincial organs to be established, the vice- president Kresimir Zubak took over as the head of the interim body, and I devoted myself to my new duties. I even set up a back-up seat of the government should it ever happen that Sarajevo could not perform this function, but my efforts were in vain because the BH army launched the attack on Travnik and then on Kakanj,which resulted in the expulsion of between 25.000 and 30.000 Croats from those municipalities. In its decision under Rule 98 bis, the Chamber mentioned the declaration that I and Mr. Stojic made on 30 June 1993 when the BH army launched its attack on Mostar. It's Prosecution exhibit 3038. What prompted the declaration, as is explained in a press release issued by the Department of Information, let me quote: "This morning at 4.45, a Muslim offensive was launched in order to capture the entire urban area. On that occasion, the speech by the 4th Corps commander Arif Pasalic was broadcast over the local radio,radio Mostar, where he said to the citizens of Mostar, Muslims, honest Croats, and loyal Serbs." End of quote. Which is probably the kind of Bosnia and Herzegovina that the Muslim side fought, at least was paying lip- service to it, the Muslim side or the BH army. Addressing the HVO, Pasalic mentions the disgraceful defeat they suffered this morning, and he quite clearly calls upon the people, I quote: "To the people, to the citizens of Mostar, understand that this is the judgement day, the day when you have to start fighting. I call upon every citizen able to bear a rifle or to throw a rock to kill the Ustasha villains because there can be no co-existence with the Ustashas. Only Muslims can live here with the honest Croats and loyal Serbs." Such a fierce speech was rare throughout the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was the only time that I felt real fear, and I spent three and a half years of the war in Mostar and in besieged Sarajevo, the two hot spots, and I entered Sarajevo at least 30 times through the makeshift tunnel that had been dug under the airport runway. As a rule, every time we got in or out we were under enemy fire. The Prlic-Stojic communique was public. It was published in the media. It calls upon Croats from the municipalities in Herzegovina to resist the aggression, and as can be seen from the declaration by the 4th Corps commander of the BH Army made on the same day, we can see from this declaration the true intentions of the BH army. This Chamber has already seen that on the very same day the Muslim party -- parties reacted condemning this aggression from the joint communique of the Muslim Democratic Party and the SDA - that's from documents 2D 082 and 1D 910 - and the president of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina informed the Secretary-General of the United Nations about this attack, urging him to take every measure necessary to prevent further aggression against the Croat people and the Croat areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina and to ensure that the peace negotiations under your auspices should continue. In this memo the Secretary-General -- just 30 seconds. In this memo, the Secretary-General was informed, I quote: "After a similar aggression in Central Bosnia, this is a renewed attempt by the Muslim army to use military force to occupy provinces that under the Vance- Owen Plan are considered Croat majority provinces," and that's document 1D 2309, and that would be all for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Prlic, how much more time would you need to finish? THE ACCUSED PRLIC: I think that I need first session, almost first session. I'm going to try to do it in an hour, but I'm not so sure. But for sure in first session tomorrow. It was very slow. I tried to, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you were slow because of Mr. Karnavas. Well, we shall finish for today. We shall resume tomorrow, as you know, at 2.15. Thank you.
